title: Finite-Element Electromagnetic Analysis and Evaluation of Antenna Performance Metrics Using a Quantum Linear System Solver
summary: Electromagnetic analysis based on the finite element method is widely used in antenna design. At higher frequencies, however, the required mesh refinement makes solving large sparse linear systems the main contributor to computational cost. Quantum linear system solvers offer a potential means of accelerating this step, but their output is a superposition state: reconstructing all components of the classical solution vector would forfeit the quantum speedup. Prior studies have proposed methods for obtaining physical quantities such as scattering cross sections and scattering parameters from the solution state. To support antenna design using fault-tolerant quantum computers, we formulate the total radiated power, the radiated power within a prescribed solid angle, and the dielectric and conductive losses as observables for efficient evaluation from a quantum solution state. These observables avoid the measurement cost of reconstructing all components of the output quantum state. We develop an end-to-end hybrid quantum--classical workflow that combines finite-element electromagnetic analysis, matrix preconditioning, a quantum linear system solver, and the evaluation of antenna design metrics. To validate the workflow, we performed numerical experiments evaluating these observables for an axisymmetric coaxially fed monopole antenna. Under idealized conditions, the relative errors in the total radiated power and the dissipated power with respect to the classical finite-element solution were on the order of $10^{-3}$, confirming the consistency of the workflow. The proposed method is expected to provide a basis for using quantum linear system solvers to evaluate antenna performance and, in the future, to design high-frequency wireless devices.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates total radiated power, radiated power within a prescribed solid angle, and dielectric/conductive losses as observables extractable efficiently from a quantum solution state, then develops an end-to-end hybrid quantum-classical workflow (FEM electromagnetic analysis, preconditioning, quantum linear system solving, metric evaluation) and validates it on an axisymmetric coaxially fed monopole antenna with relative errors on the order of 10^-3 under idealized conditions.
AI.motivation: FEM-based electromagnetic analysis for antenna design becomes dominated by large sparse linear system solving at higher frequencies due to mesh refinement. Quantum linear system solvers (QLSS) can potentially accelerate this, but their output is a superposition state, and reconstructing the full classical solution vector would negate the quantum speedup. Prior work extracted scattering cross sections and scattering parameters, but antenna-relevant metrics remained unaddressed, motivating observable formulations suited to antenna design.
AI.method: The authors express total radiated power, radiated power within a prescribed solid angle, and dielectric and conductive losses as observables computable directly from the quantum solution state, avoiding full-vector reconstruction. They construct an end-to-end hybrid quantum-classical workflow integrating finite-element electromagnetic analysis, matrix preconditioning, a quantum linear system solver, and evaluation of antenna design metrics, and test it numerically on an axisymmetric coaxially fed monopole antenna.
AI.result: In numerical experiments on the monopole antenna, under idealized conditions the relative errors in total radiated power and dissipated power relative to the classical finite-element solution were on the order of 10^-3, confirming consistency of the workflow.
AI.conclusion: The proposed observable-based formulation and hybrid workflow provide a basis for using quantum linear system solvers to evaluate antenna performance, with the prospect of supporting high-frequency wireless device design on fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Finite-resource cooling of qudits beyond thermodynamic length
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, plus 7 pages of Supplemental Material. Code and data: https://github.com/anshM123/Resonant-Collision-Cooling
summary: Cooling a quantum system with $N$ thermal machines costs more than Landauer's bound. For swap-based collision models the excess is set by thermodynamic length, which is optimal for qubits and was suggested by numerics to be optimal in general. We show that for qudits, permutations of energy eigenstates that use several resonant transitions at once do better for every spectrum, reducing the excess by up to 83% near the ground state. To second order, coherent collisions do no better, and at infinite temperature $d_M$-level machines reduce the excess by at most a factor $d_M-1$.

AI.tldr: For qudits, multi-resonance permutations of energy eigenstates beat swap-based collision models and are strictly better than thermodynamic length for every spectrum, cutting the excess cooling cost by up to 83% near the ground state; coherent collisions offer no second-order improvement, and at infinite temperature the excess reduction is capped by a factor d_M−1.
AI.motivation: Cooling with N thermal machines exceeds Landauer's bound, and for swap-based collision models this excess is fixed by thermodynamic length, previously argued (for qubits provably, otherwise numerically) to be optimal. The authors test whether this optimality survives for higher-dimensional (qudit) systems.
AI.method: Analyze collision models where machines implement permutations of the qudit energy eigenstates, including permutations employing several resonant transitions simultaneously (rather than single-transition swaps). Compare excess cost against the thermodynamic-length prediction, examine second-order (coherent) collision protocols, and derive an infinite-temperature bound for d_M-level machines.
AI.result: Multi-resonance permutations outperform thermodynamic length for every spectrum, reducing the excess by up to 83% near the ground state. Coherent collisions provide no improvement to second order. At infinite temperature, d_M-level machines reduce the excess by at most a factor d_M − 1.
AI.conclusion: Thermodynamic length is not generally optimal beyond qubits; multi-resonant permutation protocols yield strictly lower excess cooling cost, while coherence and machine dimension offer only limited or bounded gains.

title: Quantum manifestations of converse symmetry breaking
summary: Quantum synchronization holds promise in advancing quantum technologies such as sensing, communication, and computation. A key challenge in this rapidly developing field is to identify mechanisms that can promote the emergence of synchronous dynamics. Here, we show that quantum synchronization can be enhanced by introducing controlled heterogeneity in the form of coupling mismatches. Using spin van der Pol oscillators as a model system, we show that this mechanism constitutes a quantum analog of the phenomenon of converse symmetry breaking previously identified in classical oscillator networks, where a synchronous state is stabilized by explicit symmetry breaking. We quantify how quantum effects modify this behavior by tuning the degree of quantumness through variations of the spin quantum number. These findings suggest that quantum synchronization can be enhanced in experiments by harnessing rather than suppressing heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: Introducing controlled heterogeneity (coupling mismatches) can enhance quantum synchronization in spin van der Pol oscillators, constituting a quantum analog of converse symmetry breaking where explicit symmetry breaking stabilizes the synchronous state.
AI.motivation: Quantum synchronization is promising for sensing, communication, and computation, but a key open challenge is identifying mechanisms that promote the emergence of synchronous dynamics. The authors seek a controllable mechanism to enhance synchronization rather than suppress it.
AI.method: The authors use spin van der Pol oscillators as a model system and introduce controlled heterogeneity in the form of coupling mismatches. They analyze how the synchronous state is stabilized by explicit symmetry breaking, drawing an analogy to converse symmetry breaking in classical oscillator networks, and tune the degree of quantumness via the spin quantum number to quantify quantum corrections.
AI.result: Coupling mismatches (controlled heterogeneity) enhance quantum synchronization. The mechanism is shown to be a quantum analog of converse symmetry breaking, and quantum effects are found to modify this behavior, with the impact quantified as a function of the spin quantum number (degree of quantumness).
AI.conclusion: Quantum synchronization can be enhanced by harnessing rather than suppressing heterogeneity, suggesting an experimentally viable route to promote synchronous dynamics in quantum systems.

title: Spherical law for optimal layouts of random graphs
summary: Can the nodes of a random graph be placed in an auxiliary space $\mathbb{R}^{M}$ so that its connectivity becomes local? The spring electric layout is a standard algorithm to try to find such local graph layouts; we study it as a statistical-physics problem by considering the Gibbs ensemble of spring-electric layouts. For graphs with independent edges we solve the model exactly at large number of nodes $N$ and fixed embedding dimension $M$. The node positions obey a spherical law: they are uniformly distributed in an $M$-dimensional ball; for $M=2$ this is closely related to Girko's circular law. Crucially, the ground state energy is flat across all layouts with that density: an optimal layout for one graph is asymptotically optimal for any other. Optimal layouts of i.i.d. graphs are therefore frustrated liquids, macroscopically constrained but microscopically unoptimizable. We discuss relations to graph-partitioning, Laplacian eigenmaps, and dimensionality reduction, and outline how this harsh result breaks down for correlated graphs.

AI.tldr: The spring-electric layout algorithm is analyzed as a Gibbs-ensemble statistical-physics problem; for i.i.d. graphs it is solved exactly at large N and fixed M, revealing that optimal layouts follow a universal spherical law and are macroscopically constrained but microscopically unoptimizable ("frustrated liquids").
AI.motivation: Graph layouts aim to embed nodes in R^M so connectivity becomes local; the authors ask whether such an auxiliary-space embedding is meaningful, treating spring-electric layout theoretically rather than heuristically.
AI.method: Formulate the Gibbs ensemble of spring-electric layouts and solve it exactly in the large-N limit at fixed embedding dimension M, for graphs with independent edges. The resulting equilibrium node-position distribution is derived analytically and connected to Girko's circular law; relations to graph partitioning, Laplacian eigenmaps and dimensionality reduction are discussed, and the i.i.d. assumption is relaxed to correlated graphs.
AI.result: Node positions obey a spherical law—uniform distribution in an M-dimensional ball (for M=2, closely tied to Girko's circular law). Crucially, the ground-state energy is flat across all layouts with that density, so an optimal layout for one graph is asymptotically optimal for any other graph. Optimal layouts are therefore "frustrated liquids": macroscopically constrained but microscopically unoptimizable.
AI.conclusion: For i.i.d. graphs, spring-electric layout carries essentially no graph-specific information—the optimized geometry is universal. This harsh result is shown to break down for correlated graphs, which is where meaningful local layouts (and links to partitioning/eigenmaps) can emerge.

title: A Universal Approach to Hydrodynamics in Higher Dimensions via Tensor Networks
comment: 4.5 pages, 4 figures; 2 pages, 1 figure; 4 pages, 4 figures
summary: Extracting late-time hydrodynamic transport properties directly from microscopic quantum models, especially in dimensions beyond one, is believed to be classically intractable. This owes, in part, to the extensive growth of entanglement in higher dimensions and often a mismatch between geometric and tensor network locality. Here, we extend the Density Matrix Truncation (DMT) algorithm to accurately and quantitatively predict high-temperature transport coefficients (e.g. diffusion constants) in up to three dimensions. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability to capture the slow crossover dynamics characteristic of weakly broken integrability. The intuition underlying our approach is to preserve the geometrically local information crucial for hydrodynamics throughout the time evolution, despite using a one-dimensional matrix product state ansatz for higher-dimensional calculations. Our work pushes the boundary of classical computability and opens the door to benchmarking the high-temperature, late-time dynamics of generic quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: The authors extend the Density Matrix Truncation (DMT) algorithm to quantitatively predict high-temperature hydrodynamic transport coefficients, such as diffusion constants, in up to three dimensions, and to capture slow crossover dynamics from weakly broken integrability, despite using a 1D matrix product state ansatz.
AI.motivation: Extracting late-time hydrodynamic transport properties directly from microscopic quantum models in dimensions greater than one is generally considered classically intractable. This difficulty stems partly from extensive entanglement growth in higher dimensions and the frequent mismatch between geometric locality and tensor network locality.
AI.method: The authors extend the Density Matrix Truncation (DMT) algorithm to higher-dimensional settings. The core intuition is to retain the geometrically local information essential for hydrodynamics throughout the time evolution, even while employing a one-dimensional matrix product state ansatz for calculations in higher dimensions.
AI.result: DMT accurately and quantitatively predicts high-temperature transport coefficients (e.g., diffusion constants) in up to three dimensions, and also captures the slow crossover dynamics characteristic of weakly broken integrability.
AI.conclusion: The work pushes the boundary of classical computability and opens the door to benchmarking the high-temperature, late-time dynamics of generic quantum simulators.

title: Existence of the thermodynamic limit for the Hopfield model
summary: We prove that the quenched pressure of the Hopfield model with $K\simαN$ i.i.d. symmetric Rademacher patterns has a thermodynamic limit at every load $α\in(0,\infty)$, finite inverse temperature and uniform external field, with no replica-symmetry, order-parameter concentration or non-condensation hypothesis required. The limit is the supremum over $r$ of limiting pressures of mixed models with $r$ binary patterns in a Gaussian bulk. Via the Hubbard--Stratonovich representation we extract the finitely many patterns whose hidden coordinates exceed $δ\sqrt N$; a collective interpolation replaces the other binary patterns by Gaussian ones with error $O(δ^2)$ uniform in the volume, and convex concentration on the discrete cube controls the disorder-dependent choice of retained patterns. For the mixed models we prove a Gaussian hidden-spin truncation bound uniform in the volume and in an arbitrary Ising potential, and convergence for Gaussian bulks with finitely many site-field types, reducing to results of Ho and of Chen, Ho and Issa on non-convex vector spin glasses with compact spins. For Gaussian patterns we give an alternative proof of the existence result announced by Camilli, Contucci and Mingione, extended to a uniform field and an extra binary pattern. In both cases the pressure has exponentially small deviation probabilities and converges a.s.; internal energy and entropy converge wherever the limit is differentiable. An extra binary Mattis pattern admits a scalar variational reduction. At zero field the Rademacher pressure dominates the Gaussian one with an extra binary pattern, which dominates the pure Gaussian one. No explicit formula is given. The proofs were generated through extensive interaction with the AI models Claude (Opus~5.5) and ChatGPT (Sol~6.1), based on the problem formulation and guidance of the authors.

AI.tldr: The authors prove that the quenched pressure of the Hopfield model with K∼αN i.i.d. symmetric Rademacher patterns admits a thermodynamic limit for every finite load α, finite inverse temperature and uniform external field, without replica-symmetry, order-parameter concentration or non-condensation assumptions; the limit is expressed as a supremum over mixed models with r binary patterns in a Gaussian bulk.
AI.motivation: Existing results on the thermodynamic limit of the Hopfield model typically rely on restrictive hypotheses — replica symmetry, order-parameter concentration, or non-condensation of patterns. The paper aims to remove these assumptions and establish the limit in full generality at arbitrary load α∈(0,∞), finite inverse temperature and uniform external field.
AI.method: Via the Hubbard–Stratonovich representation, the finitely many patterns whose hidden coordinates exceed δ√N are extracted; a collective interpolation replaces the remaining binary patterns by Gaussian ones with error O(δ²) uniform in volume, while convex concentration on the discrete cube controls the disorder-dependent selection of retained patterns. For the mixed models, a Gaussian hidden-spin truncation bound uniform in volume and in an arbitrary Ising potential is proven, plus convergence for Gaussian bulks with finitely many site-field types, reducing to known results of Ho and of Chen–Ho–Issa on non-convex vector spin glasses with compact spins. A similar approach yields an alternative proof for Gaussian patterns, extending earlier work of Camilli–Contucci–Mingione to a uniform field and an extra binary pattern. (Proofs generated with AI model assistance.)
AI.result: A thermodynamic limit exists at every load α∈(0,∞); the limit equals the supremum over r of limiting pressures of mixed models with r binary patterns in a Gaussian bulk. The pressure exhibits exponentially small deviation probabilities and converges almost surely; internal energy and entropy converge wherever the limit is differentiable. An extra binary Mattis pattern admits a scalar variational reduction. At zero field, the Rademacher pressure dominates the Gaussian pressure with an extra binary pattern, which in turn dominates the pure Gaussian one. No explicit formula is provided.
AI.conclusion: The thermodynamic limit of the Hopfield model's quenched pressure is established under fully general conditions, without replica symmetry, concentration or non-condensation hypotheses, via a mixed-model expansion and interpolation/concentration arguments. The result unifies and extends prior analyses of Rademacher and Gaussian patterns, provides a.s. convergence with exponentially small deviations and differentiability-based convergence of energy and entropy, and yields a hierarchy of pressures at zero field, though without an explicit closed-form expression.

title: Fock-space delocalization and its control in scarred-vs-ergodic dynamics
summary: Quantum many-body scarred dynamics in Rydberg-atom arrays is characterized by revivals, in which the system repeatedly returns to its initial state despite its many-body complexity. But how extensively does the wave function explore the space of allowed configurations between revivals? We address this question by quantifying the fraction of configurations occupied during PXP dynamics initialized from the paradigmatic polarized and Néel states, which respectively exhibit thermalizing and scarred dynamics. Despite their striking revivals, dynamics from the Néel state spreads over exponentially many configurations, yet occupies a vanishing fraction of the full space in the thermodynamic limit. Dynamics from the polarized state, by contrast, occupies a finite fraction of the configuration space, close to anticoncentration and random-state statistics, although chiral symmetry limits this fraction to one third. A weak quasiperiodic field enables the polarized state to occupy half of the configuration space by lifting the constraint imposed by chiral symmetry. The Néel state, however, requires a stronger field to reach a comparable anticoncentrated regime. As the field increases further, the occupied fraction decreases for both initial states, revealing a nonmonotonic dependence of Fock-space delocalization on field strength without necessarily implying localization.

AI.tldr: This work quantifies how much of the allowed configuration (Fock) space PXP dynamics explores between revivals, showing that scarred Néel-state dynamics spreads over exponentially many configurations yet occupies a vanishing fraction in the thermodynamic limit, while thermalizing polarized-state dynamics occupies a finite fraction limited to one third by chiral symmetry.
AI.motivation: Revivals in Rydberg-atom arrays signal quantum many-body scarring, but the extent to which the wave function explores the space of allowed configurations between revivals is unclear. The authors ask whether scarred dynamics is confined to a small subspace or delocalizes broadly despite its coherent revivals.
AI.method: The authors quantify the fraction of configurations occupied during PXP dynamics initialized from the polarized and Néel states, which exhibit thermalizing and scarred dynamics respectively. They compare against anticoncentration and random-state statistics, analyze the role of chiral symmetry in constraining the occupied fraction, and apply a weak quasiperiodic field to lift the chiral constraint, tracking the occupied fraction as field strength increases.
AI.result: Néel-state dynamics spreads over exponentially many configurations yet occupies a vanishing fraction of the full space in the thermodynamic limit. Polarized-state dynamics occupies a finite fraction close to anticoncentration and random-state statistics, though chiral symmetry caps it at one third. A weak quasiperiodic field lifts the chiral constraint, letting the polarized state occupy half the configuration space; the Néel state needs a stronger field to reach a comparable anticoncentrated regime. Beyond that, the occupied fraction decreases for both states, giving nonmonotonic dependence of Fock-space delocalization on field strength without necessarily implying localization.
AI.conclusion: Revivals do not imply Fock-space confinement: scarred and thermalizing PXP dynamics differ sharply in the fraction of configuration space occupied. Chiral symmetry quantitatively bounds delocalization, quasiperiodic fields can lift it, and Fock-space delocalization depends nonmonotonically on field strength without necessarily signaling localization.

title: Topological Quantum Error-Correcting Thresholds of a Symmetry-Enriched Toric Code
summary: We study the error thresholds of a new topological quantum error-correcting code under the independent bit-flip and phase-flip noisy channel. By mapping to classical spin-glass models, we find that if Pauli X and Z errors are equally probable, the threshold of vertex syndromes is improved by 30% compared to that of the toric code, while the threshold of plaquette syndromes is lowered. Both thresholds increase when the Z component is less likely than the X component, reaching 0.5 if the Z component is absent. An analytical proof justifies this special case of perfect correctability, and a disordered version of Peierls's argument establishes a lower bound for the vertex-syndrome threshold.

AI.tldr: The vertex-syndrome error threshold of a new topological quantum code is 30% higher than the toric code under symmetric Pauli noise, and reaches 0.5 when Z errors vanish.
AI.motivation: To characterize the error-correction capability of a new topological quantum error-correcting code by determining its error thresholds under independent bit-flip and phase-flip noise, and to compare it against the well-known toric code.
AI.method: The authors map the code's error thresholds onto classical spin-glass models, using this statistical-mechanical correspondence to compute vertex- and plaquette-syndrome thresholds. They provide an analytical proof for the special case with no Z noise and derive a lower bound on the vertex-syndrome threshold via a disordered version of Peierls's argument.
AI.result: For equal Pauli X and Z error probabilities, the vertex-syndrome threshold improves by 30% over the toric code, whereas the plaquette-syndrome threshold is reduced. Both thresholds increase when Z errors are less probable than X errors, reaching 0.5 when the Z component is absent.
AI.conclusion: The new code offers enhanced vertex-syndrome correctability relative to the toric code under symmetric noise, with perfect correctability in the pure bit-flip limit, analytically justified and supported by a rigorous lower bound.

title: Liouvillian spectral snapshots: A reduced-subspace approach for time-dependent and noisy open quantum systems
summary: Driven-dissipative quantum devices are routinely operated with time-dependent drives and exposed to temporally correlated classical noise. When these perturbations vary on timescales comparable to the system's intrinsic dynamics, rotating-wave and Markovian approximations can fail, making effective static descriptions unreliable. As a result, accurately modeling systems in this regime often relies on simulating the full time-dependent master equation. This is particularly demanding for processes requiring long integration times, such as rare switching between metastable states, or for stochastic perturbations requiring averaging over many noise realizations. To address these challenges, we introduce Liouvillian spectral snapshots (LSS), a reduced-basis method that enables efficient simulation of such systems by projecting the master equation onto a low-dimensional subspace capturing their coarse-grained dynamics. LSS constructs this subspace by computing the slowly decaying, low-frequency eigenoperators of the Liouvillian at a few adaptively sampled perturbation values and compressing them into a common basis. This basis is built once and can be reused across noise realizations and perturbation parameters, reducing the cost of ensemble averages and parameter sweeps.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Liouvillian spectral snapshots (LSS), a reduced-basis method that projects a time-dependent master equation onto a low-dimensional subspace built from slowly decaying, low-frequency Liouvillian eigenoperators sampled at a few adaptive perturbation values, enabling efficient simulation of driven-dissipative quantum devices under time-dependent drives and correlated noise.
AI.motivation: Driven-dissipative quantum devices are operated with time-dependent drives and temporally correlated classical noise, and when these perturbations vary on timescales comparable to the intrinsic dynamics, rotating-wave and Markovian approximations fail, making effective static descriptions unreliable. Accurate modeling then requires simulating the full time-dependent master equation, which is prohibitively expensive for long integration times (e.g., rare switching between metastable states) and for stochastic perturbations needing averaging over many noise realizations.
AI.method: LSS is a reduced-basis method that projects the master equation onto a low-dimensional subspace capturing the coarse-grained dynamics. It constructs this subspace by computing slowly decaying, low-frequency eigenoperators of the Liouvillian at a few adaptively sampled perturbation values and compressing them into a common basis. This basis is built once and reused across noise realizations and perturbation parameters.
AI.result: The method enables efficient simulation of driven-dissipative systems in regimes where rotating-wave and Markovian approximations break down, reducing the cost of ensemble averages over noise realizations and of parameter sweeps, and making long-time dynamics such as rare switching between metastable states tractable. (The abstract emphasizes efficiency gains qualitatively rather than reporting specific numerical speedups.)
AI.conclusion: LSS provides a practical reduced-basis framework for accurate, efficient simulation of time-dependent driven-dissipative quantum dynamics under correlated noise, with a reusable basis that amortizes cost across ensemble averages and parameter sweeps.

title: Beyond the Kubo formula: unification of adiabatic and isothermal response in quantum systems
summary: The static limit of the Kubo susceptibility describes the adiabatic response of an isolated quantum system, in which energy-level occupations remain unchanged, and generally differs from the isothermal susceptibility, where these occupations readjust to thermal equilibrium. In this work, we introduce a single dynamical framework in which the adiabatic and isothermal responses arise naturally as two distinct limiting regimes. This can be done by considering explicitly an open system version of the Kubo approach in which the dissipation is governed by a typical thermalization rate of the system. By exchanging the order of the static limit and of the vanishing thermalization rate limit, the protocol yields either the adiabatic or isothermal response. This protocol has a solid physical motivation in terms of the thermalization dynamics and is valid for generic systems. We apply it to the case of the magnetic response of the electron gas and reproduce the expected results.

AI.tldr: The authors unify adiabatic and isothermal Kubo susceptibilities within a single open-system framework governed by a thermalization rate, where the order of the static and vanishing-dissipation limits selects one response or the other, validated on the magnetic response of the electron gas.
AI.motivation: The static Kubo susceptibility (adiabatic, fixed occupations) generally differs from the isothermal susceptibility (occupations re-equilibrate), yet there is no unified dynamical framework connecting the two; the paper aims to bridge this gap with a physically motivated protocol.
AI.method: An open-system version of the Kubo approach is introduced in which dissipation is governed by a typical thermalization rate. The static limit and the vanishing-thermalization-rate limit are taken in different orders: one ordering yields the adiabatic response, the other the isothermal response.
AI.result: The ordering of the two limits reproduces the adiabatic and isothermal responses respectively, providing a solid interpretation in terms of thermalization dynamics. Applied to the magnetic response of the electron gas, the protocol recovers the expected results (Pauli/Landau-type adiabatic and isothermal magnetic susceptibilities).
AI.conclusion: Adiabatic and isothermal responses emerge as two distinct limiting regimes of a single open-system Kubo framework; the protocol is general and physically grounded, with the electron-gas magnetic response as a confirming application.

title: Distilling Knowledge from Search: Decoder Model Factory for Quantum LDPC Codes
summary: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. GraphMP uses local message passing to keep computation scalable as the decoding graph grows. Guided by its predictions, beam search progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading additional decoding time for lower logical error rates. We develop the decoder model factory as a paradigm for training successive models on experience generated by earlier models during decoding. Model-guided search supplies verified trajectories for knowledge distillation, folding computation spent on decoding into reusable training data. Repeated collection and distillation improve the decoder across generations and adapt its strategy as the noise changes. These results motivate a coupled quantum--classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning renews the models from operating experience. The long-term vision is a scalable decoder model factory that produces high-performance, low-latency decoders and continually adapts them to evolving quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: GraphMP is a transferable learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum LDPC codes, paired with a "decoder model factory" paradigm that folds decoding-time computation into reusable training data via model-guided beam search and knowledge distillation.
AI.motivation: Quantum LDPC decoders must remain accurate and scalable across diverse code families, sizes, physical error rates, and noise models, yet learned decoders typically require fine-tuning per setting. The work targets decoders that transfer without retraining and continually improve from operating experience.
AI.method: GraphMP employs local message passing to keep computation scalable as the decoding graph grows; its predictions guide beam search that progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading decoding time for lower logical error rates. A decoder model factory trains successive models on experience generated by earlier models: model-guided search yields verified trajectories used for knowledge distillation, and repeated collection-distillation cycles renew the models and adapt their strategy as noise changes.
AI.result: The decoder transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models; beam search guided by learned predictions lowers logical error rates at the cost of additional decoding time; and generation-over-generation collection and distillation improve the decoder, adapting it as the noise changes.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate a coupled quantum–classical architecture with two interacting cycles—fast decoding for protection and slower learning for model renewal—toward a scalable decoder model factory yielding high-performance, low-latency, continually adaptive decoders for evolving quantum hardware.

title: Witnessing and quantifying stellar rank with the Wigner function
summary: Quantifying non-Gaussianity is essential for assessing the computational power of bosonic quantum systems. We introduce a framework to witness and quantify non-Gaussianity from displaced parity measurements, and we directly apply it to experimental data obtained with superconducting cavities. Our method estimates fidelities with target pure states from the displaced parity measurements, enabling certification of non-Gaussianity via the stellar rank. We further introduce refined witnesses computed by measuring the value of the Wigner function at a few points, providing efficient certification tools outperforming existing ones. Applying these techniques to Fock, binomial, cat, and GKP experimental data, we rigorously certify non-Gaussian resources and establish a stellar rank of $8$ for a GKP state, setting a new benchmark across all quantum platforms. Our methods enable a rigorous quantification of non-Gaussian quantum resources directly applicable to superconducting devices.

AI.tldr: A framework witnesses and quantifies non-Gaussianity using displaced parity measurements, certifying non-Gaussian resources in superconducting cavities and establishing a stellar rank of 8 for a GKP state.
AI.motivation: Quantifying non-Gaussianity is essential for assessing the computational power of bosonic quantum systems, yet rigorous and experimentally applicable certification tools are needed.
AI.method: The approach estimates fidelities with target pure states from displaced parity measurements, certifying non-Gaussianity via the stellar rank, and introduces refined witnesses based on the Wigner function value at a few points.
AI.result: Applied to Fock, binomial, cat, and GKP experimental data, the techniques rigorously certify non-Gaussian resources and establish a stellar rank of 8 for a GKP state, a new benchmark across all quantum platforms; the refined witnesses outperform existing ones.
AI.conclusion: The methods enable rigorous quantification of non-Gaussian quantum resources directly applicable to superconducting devices.

title: Electronic-Structure-Informed Many-Body Encoding for Quantum Machine Learning
summary: Data encoding is a central challenge in quantum machine learning (QML), as it determines how classical information is mapped onto quantum states and influences the expressive power and efficiency of parameterized quantum circuits. Here, we introduce a physics-informed quantum encoding strategy that exploits the intrinsic many-body structure of electronic systems to establish a direct correspondence between the body order of input descriptors and the locality of quantum gates. Specifically, $n$-body electronic descriptors obtained from a single mean-field electronic-structure calculation are encoded through $n$-qubit gates, yielding a systematic hierarchy of quantum circuits with increasing many-body expressivity. Using reduced-density-matrix descriptors, we construct quantum machine-learning models incorporating one- through four-body encodings and benchmark their performance in predicting electron-correlation energies along bond-stretching potential energy surfaces. We demonstrate that increasing the body order of the encoding systematically improves prediction accuracy toward the full configuration interaction limit. Remarkably, disconnected many-particle densities constructed from lower-order electronic information achieve accuracy comparable to explicitly correlated two-particle densities in key cases, providing a computationally inexpensive route to higher-body quantum encodings. These findings establish a connection between the many-body structure of classical data and the design of quantum feature maps, offering a systematic, physically interpretable framework for enhancing the expressivity and predictive performance of quantum machine-learning circuits.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed quantum encoding maps the body order of electronic descriptors onto the locality of n-qubit gates, and higher-body encodings systematically improve prediction of electron-correlation energies toward the FCI limit.
AI.motivation: Data encoding determines how classical information is mapped onto quantum states, controlling expressivity and efficiency of parameterized quantum circuits. The authors seek a physically interpretable encoding scheme for QML in electronic-structure problems.
AI.method: Descriptors from a single mean-field calculation are encoded with n-qubit gates, giving a hierarchy of circuits with increasing many-body expressivity. Using reduced-density-matrix (RDM) descriptors, QML models with one- through four-body encodings are trained to predict electron-correlation energies along bond-stretching potential energy surfaces.
AI.result: Increasing the body order of the encoding systematically improves accuracy toward the full configuration interaction (FCI) limit. Disconnected many-particle densities built from lower-order information match explicitly correlated two-particle densities in key cases.
AI.conclusion: The work links the many-body structure of classical data to quantum feature-map design, providing a systematic, physically interpretable framework for boosting expressivity and predictive performance of QML circuits; disconnected densities offer a cheap route to higher-body encodings.

title: Predictive Maintenance at the Edge: An Embedded Anomaly Detection Pipeline Trained with Quantum Optimization
summary: This article presents a predictive-maintenance pipeline that detects anomalies in bearings from vibration signals, adapted for deployment at the edge on low-cost microcontrollers, and that uses quantum optimization in two steps of its training. The pipeline consists of a step of vibration feature extraction and a step of classification with a one-class support vector machine (OCSVM). The features are selected by minimum redundancy and maximum relevance (mRMR) with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), under a limit on computing time. The OCSVM is adapted for inference at the edge without floating-point operations and is trained by a variational quantum algorithm with Pauli-correlation encoding (PCE). In small-scale tests on a simulator, with the Paderborn bearing dataset, the VQE found the optimal selection in 36% of the runs with Adam, and PCE chose better support vectors than chance, until a classical local search made the two equal. A classical baseline, the usual OCSVM trained by SMO with its weights rounded, matched them without any search.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an edge-deployable predictive-maintenance pipeline for bearing anomaly detection that combines vibration feature extraction, mRMR feature selection driven by VQE, and a float-free OCSVM trained via a PCE-based variational quantum algorithm, benchmarked against a classical SMO baseline on the Paderborn dataset.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to bring predictive maintenance of bearings to low-cost microcontrollers at the edge while exploring whether quantum optimization can meaningfully improve two training steps, despite tight constraints on compute time and integer-only inference.
AI.method: The pipeline has two stages: (1) vibration feature extraction, with feature selection by mRMR optimized via VQE under a computing-time budget (e.g., Adam optimizer); (2) classification by an OCSVM adapted for edge inference without floating-point operations, trained by a variational quantum algorithm with Pauli-correlation encoding (PCE). Evaluation is on a simulator with the Paderborn bearing dataset in small-scale tests.
AI.result: VQE found the optimal feature selection in 36% of runs with Adam; PCE selected better support vectors than chance but only until a classical local search equalized them. A classical baseline (SMO-trained OCSVM with rounded weights) matched both without any search.
AI.conclusion: The quantum-assisted steps did not outperform a simple classical baseline in these small-scale tests, indicating limited practical advantage of the proposed quantum optimization for this edge predictive-maintenance task as evaluated.

title: Colloquium: Quantum information processing with ensembles of identical particles
comment: 41 pages, 30 figures, 1 table. Colloquium submitted to Review of Modern Physics
summary: Identical particles underpin most quantum technologies, but the role of indistinguishability in these processes extends far beyond the symmetrization of many-particle states. This Colloquium presents a unified operational perspective on how particle identity, indistinguishability, exchange statistics, and many-particle interference can instead be harnessed as resources for quantum information processing. We first clarify the notions of entanglement and indistinguishability for identical particles, emphasizing their dependence on the accessible measurements and information. We then review how spatial overlap, multiparticle interference, and path identity enable the generation, extraction, protection, and distillation of coherence and entanglement. Their applications to quantum metrology and imaging, state discrimination, teleportation, entanglement swapping, and quantum cloning are examined. Finally, we discuss the thermodynamic role of indistinguishability, from the Gibbs paradox to quantum thermal machines and statistics-driven engines. Across these settings, indistinguishability emerges as a controllable, task-dependent resource whose benefits are determined by state preparation, exchange statistics, interference, and measurement constraints.

AI.tldr: This Colloquium reviews how particle identity, indistinguishability, exchange statistics, and many-particle interference act as controllable, task-dependent resources for quantum information processing, metrology, imaging, thermodynamics, and related tasks.
AI.motivation: Identical particles underpin most quantum technologies, yet the role of indistinguishability extends beyond simple symmetrization of many-particle states. The paper aims to unify the understanding of how indistinguishability can be harnessed as a resource rather than treated merely as a constraint.
AI.method: The authors present a unified operational perspective: first clarifying entanglement and indistinguishability for identical particles in terms of accessible measurements and information; then reviewing how spatial overlap, multiparticle interference, and path identity enable generation, extraction, protection, and distillation of coherence and entanglement.
AI.result: The framework is connected to applications in quantum metrology and imaging, state discrimination, teleportation, entanglement swapping, and quantum cloning, and extended to thermodynamics—from the Gibbs paradox to quantum thermal machines and statistics-driven engines.
AI.conclusion: Indistinguishability emerges as a controllable, task-dependent resource whose benefits depend on state preparation, exchange statistics, interference, and measurement constraints.

title: Clifford synthesis is NP-complete
summary:
We show that the problem of synthesizing a quantum circuit for a given Clifford operator using at most a specified amount of resources is NP-complete for several resource models of practical interest.
  Specifically, we study synthesis of a given Clifford operator using single-qubit Clifford gates and two-qubit Clifford gates, with full qubit connectivity and no additional ancilla qubits. With single-qubit gates free and CNOT as the only two-qubit gate, we show that deciding whether a given target admits an implementation using at most a specified number of CNOT gates is NP-complete, and we show that the problem remains NP-complete when any two-qubit Clifford gate is allowed and the budget counts all such gates. Moreover, we show that both results continue to hold when SWAP gates may be inserted for free, and when single-qubit gates are also considered part of the budget.
  In each case, we build on recent work by Li and Guan and show that there are polynomial-time reductions from Hamiltonian path in grid graphs to these decision problems, using a number of qubits quadratic in the number of grid vertices.

AI.tldr: Synthesizing a given Clifford operator with at most a specified number of resources is NP-complete under several practical resource models, including CNOT-only budgeting, arbitrary two-qubit Clifford gate budgeting, free SWAP insertion, and counting single-qubit gates.
AI.motivation: Quantum circuit synthesis for Clifford operators is central to fault-tolerant and near-term quantum computing, where resource counts (gate budgets) directly govern feasibility. Determining the computational hardness of deciding whether a target Clifford operator admits a resource-bounded implementation clarifies the complexity landscape of practical synthesis.
AI.method: The authors reduce from Hamiltonian path in grid graphs to the resource-bounded Clifford synthesis decision problems. The constructions use a number of qubits quadratic in the number of grid vertices and build on recent work by Li and Guan.
AI.result: Deciding whether a target Clifford operator can be implemented with at most a specified number of CNOT gates (single-qubit gates free, full connectivity, no ancillas) is NP-complete. It remains NP-complete when any two-qubit Clifford gate is permitted and the budget counts all such gates, and under variants with free SWAP gates and with single-qubit gates included in the budget.
AI.conclusion: Resource-bounded synthesis of Clifford operators is computationally intractable (NP-complete) across multiple natural resource models, implying that efficient exact synthesis likely requires heuristics or restricted problem instances.

title: Optical Quantum Memory Processing for Quantum Hashing
summary: Sender authentication is an important requirement for secure quantum communication networks. We propose programmable photon-echo quantum memory processing of a multi-time-bin photonic qudit for implementing a quantum-hash-based verification protocol. In this approach, using QM, sender (Alice) generates a quantum hash state by transforming a single stored photonic wave packet into the programmable photonic qudit. Bob's memory coherently maps the received time-bin photonic qudit into a single output mode according to phase encoding. Our scheme relies on a time-resolved coherent detection method introduced here, in which the coherent responses from individual time-bins are sequentially accumulated within Bob's spin coherence prior to the final sender verification. The key advantage of this coherent detection for quantum hashing is shown, and its potential applications are also discussed. The performed analysis demonstrates that experimentally verified parameters of contemporary optical quantum memories enable a proof of principle realization of the proposed architecture. These results reveal an additional role for quantum memories, serving not only as synchronization and repeater resources for long-distance quantum communication, but also as active elements for quantum hashing in conventional quantum key distribution systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using programmable photon-echo quantum memory to process a multi-time-bin photonic qudit as a quantum hash for sender authentication in quantum communication networks.
AI.motivation: Secure quantum communication networks require sender authentication. Quantum memories (QMs) have so far served mainly as synchronization and repeater resources; the authors seek an additional functional role for them in cryptographic verification.
AI.method: A quantum-hash-based verification protocol is implemented via programmable photon-echo QM processing of a multi-time-bin photonic qudit. Alice transforms a single stored photonic wave packet into a programmable photonic qudit (the quantum hash state). Bob's memory coherently maps the received time-bin qudit into a single output mode according to phase encoding, using a time-resolved coherent detection method in which coherent responses from individual time-bins are sequentially accumulated within Bob's spin coherence prior to final verification.
AI.result: The key advantage of coherent detection for quantum hashing is demonstrated. Analysis shows that experimentally verified parameters of contemporary optical quantum memories suffice for a proof-of-principle realization of the proposed architecture.
AI.conclusion: Quantum memories can act not only as synchronization and repeater resources for long-distance quantum communication but also as active elements for quantum hashing in conventional QKD systems; potential applications are discussed.

title: Hypergraph cycle enumeration for efficient inference of planted k-XOR with smooth trade-off
summary: We introduce hypergraph cycle enumeration (HCE), a simple spectral framework for detecting and recovering planted signals in noisy hypergraph inference problems. We study HCE on one representative problem from this class, namely planted noisy k-XOR, also known as sparse Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). Both theoretically and empirically, HCE achieves comparable recovery behavior to Kikuchi method, matching Kikuchi hierarchy. We identify parameter regimes where HCE outperforms Kikuchi method, showing that neither algorithm is universally better. We also show a subquadratic quantum speedup for HCE by replacing one of the algorithm's steps with a quantum walk. Our classical and quantum algorithms do not refute the quartic quantum speedup of quantum Kikuchi method, which remains valid for the practically relevant regime of large size and high noise strength.

AI.tldr: HCE is a simple spectral framework for planted signal recovery in noisy hypergraph inference, studied on planted noisy k-XOR (sparse LPN), matching Kikuchi hierarchy performance, sometimes outperforming it, and admitting a subquadratic quantum speedup.
AI.motivation: Detecting and recovering planted signals in noisy hypergraph inference problems is challenging; existing methods like the Kikuchi hierarchy are complex, and there is interest in simpler spectral approaches and understanding their theoretical and practical trade-offs, including quantum acceleration.
AI.method: The authors introduce hypergraph cycle enumeration (HCE), a simple spectral algorithm based on enumerating hypergraph cycles. They analyze HCE theoretically and empirically on planted noisy k-XOR (sparse LPN), compare it against the Kikuchi method, identify parameter regimes favoring each, and obtain a quantum version by replacing one algorithmic step with a quantum walk.
AI.result: HCE achieves recovery behavior comparable to the Kikuchi method, matching the Kikuchi hierarchy. There exist parameter regimes where HCE outperforms Kikuchi, showing neither is universally better. A subquadratic quantum speedup for HCE is obtained via a quantum walk replacement. Neither the classical nor quantum HCE refutes the quartic quantum speedup of the quantum Kikuchi method, which remains valid for large size and high noise.
AI.conclusion: HCE is a competitive, simpler spectral alternative to Kikuchi methods for planted noisy k-XOR, with complementary strengths depending on the regime, and it supports a subquadratic quantum speedup while leaving the quartic quantum Kikuchi advantage intact in practically relevant large-size, high-noise settings.

title: Variational Programs with Open Clocks
summary: Variational quantum algorithms leave the durations of Hamiltonian evolutions open for a classical optimizer to set. We present VHamilton, a minimal extension of the Hamilton quantum programming language in which such durations are open clocks: one program denotes a family of Hamiltonian trajectories, and a valuation fills its clocks with exact dyadic times, so that each instance is an ordinary Hamilton program that compiles to circuits as before. Because the semantics stays exact and affine in the clocks, the Hamiltonian structure of a variational program remainsavail able for reasoning about every valuation at once. Equivalence becomes a finite calculation, which we mechanize in Agda for a fragment and use to prove the VHamilton form of the compiler rewrite "rzz(t) = cx; rz(t); cx" for every clock value. We then show what the same structure supports in a two-qubit chemistry eigensolver written in VHamilton and run through a Haskell prototype. It supports a fusion of commuting blocks, a closed form and an expressibility proof for the ansatz, and an exact split of the error between the precision of the target and that of the clocks, with a priori bounds. It also supports a coordinate search whose queries per sweep, fixed by the spectra of the generators, do not grow with the precision. On the benchmark this search reaches the numerically verified optimum of a grid of 134 million valuations in 53 energy queries. It finds the grid optimum in only 21 of 30 validation settings, however, so the gain is conditional, not a global-optimization guarantee.

AI.tldr: VHamilton extends the Hamilton language so Hamiltonian evolution durations become "open clocks," letting one variational program denote a family of trajectories whose instances are ordinary Hamilton programs. Exact affine semantics make equivalence a finite calculation, enabling verified compiler rewrites, ansatz analysis, and an efficient coordinate search for a chemistry eigensolver.
AI.motivation: Variational quantum algorithms expose Hamiltonian evolution durations to a classical optimizer, but existing languages treat these durations as concrete parameters, obscuring the Hamiltonian structure and preventing reasoning that covers all parameter valuations at once.
AI.method: Durations are modeled as open clocks filled by exact dyadic valuations; program semantics stays exact and affine in clocks. Equivalence is mechanized in Agda for a fragment, proving the rewrite rzz(t)=cx;rz(t);cx for all clock values. A two-qubit chemistry eigensolver is written in VHamilton and run via a Haskell prototype, supporting commuting-block fusion, a closed-form ansatz with expressibility proof, and an exact split of error between target precision and clock precision with a priori bounds.
AI.result: A coordinate search whose queries per sweep, fixed by generator spectra, do not grow with precision reaches the numerically verified optimum of a 134-million-valuation grid in 53 energy queries, but finds the grid optimum in only 21 of 30 validation settings.
AI.conclusion: The exact affine clock semantics preserves Hamiltonian structure for reasoning over all valuations, yielding verified rewrites, ansatz analysis, and precision-independent search. The observed gains are conditional rather than a global-optimization guarantee.

title: Preparation of a Laughlin-like fractional Chern insulator on a superconducting quantum processor
summary: Fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) are lattice analogues of fractional quantum Hall states, hosting topological order and fractionalized anyonic excitations. Their realization poses a demanding target for quantum simulation. Here, we realize a bosonic FCI on an IBM Nighthawk superconducting quantum processor using classically optimized variational circuits. We target a Laughlin-like state that is an exact zero-energy ground state of a long-range parent Hamiltonian on a torus, eliminating physical edges and providing a favorable geometry for accessing fractional quantum Hall physics in a small system. On a $4\times4$ qubit lattice, we prepare both the four-boson FCI ground state and a three-boson state hosting two quasiholes. Measurements of particle densities and correlations reproduce the characteristic structure of the target states, while reconstructed chiral magnetization currents resolve the circulating current pattern associated with the quasiholes. The preparation of these strongly correlated topological states with shallow circuits establishes a route toward the digital simulation and manipulation of fractionalized excitations, including measurements of topological invariants and anyonic braiding.

AI.tldr: A bosonic fractional Chern insulator (Laughlin-like state) and a two-quasihole state are prepared on a 4×4 qubit lattice of an IBM Nighthawk superconducting processor using classically optimized variational circuits, with measured densities, correlations, and chiral currents confirming the target topological structure.
AI.motivation: Fractional Chern insulators realize lattice analogues of fractional quantum Hall states with topological order and fractionalized anyons, but preparing them is a demanding quantum-simulation target. The authors seek a small, edge-free geometry (torus) whose target state is an exact zero-energy ground state of a long-range parent Hamiltonian, making it accessible with shallow circuits on near-term hardware.
AI.method: Use classically optimized variational circuits on an IBM Nighthawk superconducting quantum processor to prepare, on a 4×4 qubit lattice, (i) the four-boson FCI ground state and (ii) a three-boson state hosting two quasiholes. The target is a Laughlin-like state that is an exact zero-energy ground state of a long-range parent Hamiltonian on a torus. Readout includes particle-density and correlation measurements, plus reconstruction of chiral magnetization currents from the prepared states.
AI.result: The prepared states reproduce the characteristic density and correlation structure of the target FCI and quasihole states, and the reconstructed chiral magnetization currents resolve the circulating current pattern associated with the quasiholes—direct evidence of the fractionalized excitations.
AI.conclusion: Strongly correlated topological states, including quasihole excitations, can be prepared with shallow variational circuits on current superconducting hardware, establishing a route toward digital simulation and manipulation of fractionalized excitations such as topological-invariant measurements and anyonic braiding.

title: Vacuum amplification across a programmable bosonic Bogoliubov stability boundary in a trapped-ion chain
summary: A quantum oscillator always carries vacuum fluctuations, and modulating its parameters converts them into correlated pairs of real quanta. This vacuum amplification underlies squeezed light and Hawking radiation. In a closed quadratic system, pair creation competes with the energy splitting of the modes, and growth turns exponential only once pairing overcomes the splitting. Here we realize this competition in two motional modes of a trapped-ion chain. A two-mode-squeezing drive creates the pairs, and a beam-splitter coupling splits the motion into two coupled modes at different frequencies. The two rates are tuned and calibrated independently. Starting near the motional ground state, we cross the stability boundary in two ways. First, with the drive at the sum of the two bare-mode frequencies, the phonon number stays bounded until the pairing rate exceeds the splitting and grows exponentially beyond it. Second, tuning the drive into resonance with one coupled mode lowers the threshold to zero, and only that mode is amplified into a squeezed vacuum. Separate control of the two interactions makes the threshold for vacuum amplification programmable. This control can be used to simulate particle creation and quantum phase transitions, and to operate parametrically driven bosonic devices close to their stability limit.

AI.tldr: A trapped-ion experiment realizes the competition between pair creation and mode splitting that governs vacuum amplification, crossing the stability threshold in two independently tunable ways.
AI.motivation: Vacuum fluctuations of a quantum oscillator can be converted into correlated real quanta by modulating its parameters (squeezed light, Hawking radiation). In a closed quadratic system, growth becomes exponential only when the pairing rate overcomes the energy splitting; this competition has not been directly and controllably realized.
AI.method: Two motional modes of a trapped-ion chain are used. A two-mode-squeezing drive generates pairs, while a beam-splitter coupling splits the motion into two coupled modes at different frequencies. The two rates are tuned and calibrated independently. Starting near the motional ground state, the stability boundary is crossed in two configurations: (1) drive at the sum of the two bare-mode frequencies; (2) drive tuned into resonance with one coupled mode.
AI.result: With the drive at the sum frequency, the phonon number remains bounded until the pairing rate exceeds the splitting, then grows exponentially. When the drive is resonant with one coupled mode, the threshold drops to zero and only that mode is amplified into a squeezed vacuum.
AI.conclusion: Independent control of the two interactions makes the threshold for vacuum amplification programmable, enabling simulation of particle creation and quantum phase transitions and operation of parametrically driven bosonic devices near their stability limit.

title: Quantum Vehicle Routing Problem: a smart initialization strategy for ill-conditioned optimization landscapes
summary: With the expansion of complex transport infrastructure, new paths for linking different destinations have emerged, allowing the definition of multiple routes. The introduction of new roads may also lead to disruptions in traffic flow. This problem can be generalized into a special case of VRP, which aims to find the optimal route for a fleet of vehicles within a network of destinations. Finding solutions to this problem requires an exponential number of operations, hindering the ability of exact solvers to deal with large instances, which must therefore be tackled using heuristics, often leading to suboptimal results. Quantum-based algorithms may allow us to find exact solutions in polynomial time with high probability, offering a potential future alternative to classical solvers and in this work, we focus on the QAOA. Our novel contributions are a parameter-initialization strategy that improves the convergence probability and the integration of the subtour constraints directly into the optimization without using additional qubits by employing an approximation of exponential equality constraints. We believe that our results pave the way for effectively solving instances of VRP using quantum-based solutions, leveraging the space-efficient problem encoding and our initialization strategy, which limits the effect of barren-plateau under random parameter initialization.

AI.tldr: A QAOA-based approach for the Vehicle Routing Problem that adopts a space-efficient encoding, a parameter-initialization strategy to mitigate barren plateaus, and integrates subtour constraints into optimization without extra qubits.
AI.motivation: Complex transport networks create many possible routes and potential traffic disruptions, generalizing to a VRP special case. Exact solvers require exponential operations and fail on large instances, while heuristics often give suboptimal results. Quantum algorithms may yield exact solutions in polynomial time with high probability, offering an alternative to classical solvers; the work focuses on QAOA.
AI.method: Formulate the routing problem as a VRP special case and solve it with QAOA. Contribute (1) a parameter-initialization strategy that improves convergence probability and counters barren-plateau effects of random initialization, and (2) an approximation of exponential equality constraints that embeds subtour constraints directly into the optimization without additional qubits, giving a space-efficient problem encoding.
AI.result: The proposed initialization strategy improves convergence probability, and the constraint-integration scheme enforces subtour constraints with a space-efficient encoding requiring no extra qubits, limiting barren-plateau effects under random parameter initialization.
AI.conclusion: The results are positioned as a step toward effectively solving VRP instances with quantum-based solutions, combining space-efficient encoding and the proposed initialization strategy.

title: Entangled Measurement Outcomes for Optimal Postselection in Quantum Batteries
summary: Postselection can enhance the performance of a selected quantum battery branch, raising the question of whether the optimum can always be achieved by product measurements on the auxiliary subsystems. For battery auxiliary states obtained by mixing a pure state with global white noise of strength p, the conditional ergotropy reduces to a generalized Rayleigh quotient. For 0<p<1, product postselection attains the joint optimum if and only if the eigenspace associated with the largest generalized eigenvalue contains a product vector. For two auxiliary qubits, a strict product-joint gap therefore occurs precisely when this eigenspace is one dimensional and spanned by an entangled vector. Noisy W and GHZ states display qualitatively different behavior: the three qubit W state exhibits a strict gap throughout 0<p<1, whereas the three qubit GHZ state admits a product optimum. For interacting two qubit batteries, the optimal postselection can switch from a Bell outcome to a product outcome as the coupling strength is varied. By contrast, the outcome averaged capacity and ergotropy are independent of the measurement basis, showing that the joint measurement advantage is genuinely postselective.

AI.tldr: Postselection can boost a selected quantum battery branch, and product postselection attains the joint optimum iff the top generalized eigenspace contains a product vector; for two qubits a strict product-joint gap occurs only when that eigenspace is one-dimensional and spanned by an entangled vector.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the optimal postselected quantum battery performance can always be reached with product measurements on the auxiliary subsystems, i.e., whether joint (entangled) measurements are ever strictly necessary.
AI.method: For battery auxiliary states formed by mixing a pure state with global white noise of strength p, the conditional ergotropy is expressed as a generalized Rayleigh quotient. Product postselection is then analyzed via the generalized eigenvalue problem: optimality of product measurements is tied to whether the largest generalized eigenspace contains a product vector. Two-qubit, noisy W/GHZ, and interacting two-qubit battery cases are examined.
AI.result: For 0<p<1, product postselection attains the joint optimum iff the largest generalized eigenspace contains a product vector. For two auxiliary qubits, a strict product-joint gap arises precisely when this eigenspace is one-dimensional and entangled. The noisy three-qubit W state shows a strict gap for all 0<p<1, whereas the three-qubit GHZ state admits a product optimum. For interacting two-qubit batteries, the optimal postselection can switch from a Bell outcome to a product outcome as coupling strength varies.
AI.conclusion: Joint-measurement advantages in postselected quantum batteries are genuinely postselective: outcome-averaged capacity and ergotropy are independent of the measurement basis, so the advantage exists only conditionally. Product measurements suffice except in identifiable entangled-eigenspace conditions, and W vs. GHZ states exhibit qualitatively different behavior.

title: Probing Operator Spreading with Local Quantum Fluctuations
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures. Includes Supplemental Material. Comments are welcome
summary: Measuring out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) is experimentally challenging, often requiring effective reversal of many-body dynamics. Here, we propose an alternative approach to probing operator spreading through local quantum fluctuations, using only forward evolution and local measurements. Motivated by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, we introduce a differential local variance and establish a rigorous bound connecting it to operator noncommutativity. For a ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain in the single-magnon regime, we derive an exact relation between the local variance and a squared-commutator OTOC. In integrable and nonintegrable Ising chains, the differential variance and OTOCs reveal qualitatively consistent propagation fronts. Our results establish local quantum fluctuations as an experimentally accessible, state-dependent, and complementary diagnostic of operator spreading.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes probing operator spreading via local quantum fluctuations measured with only forward evolution and local measurements, introducing a "differential local variance" rigorously bounded by operator noncommutativity, and showing—via exact relations and consistent propagation fronts—that it serves as an experimentally accessible proxy for OTOCs.
AI.motivation: Measuring out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) is experimentally difficult because it typically requires effective reversal of many-body dynamics. The authors seek an alternative, experimentally feasible diagnostic of operator spreading that avoids time reversal and relies solely on forward evolution and local measurements.
AI.method: Motivated by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, the authors introduce a differential local variance and prove a rigorous bound linking it to operator noncommutativity. For a ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain in the single-magnon regime, they derive an exact relation between the local variance and a squared-commutator OTOC. They then compare the differential variance with OTOCs in both integrable and nonintegrable Ising chains.
AI.result: The differential local variance is rigorously bounded by operator noncommutativity. In the single-magnon Heisenberg chain, an exact relation holds between local variance and the squared-commutator OTOC. In both integrable and nonintegrable Ising chains, the differential variance and OTOCs exhibit qualitatively consistent propagation fronts.
AI.conclusion: Local quantum fluctuations—captured by the differential local variance—provide an experimentally accessible, state-dependent, and complementary diagnostic of operator spreading, circumventing the need for many-body dynamics reversal.

title: Encoded reversible addition in constant Toffoli depth
summary: We show that reversible in-place quantum addition modulo $2^n-1$ can be implemented in constant Toffoli depth using $O(n)$ space, provided that the variables are encoded in a certain non-standard form. Using measurement-based uncomputation, the Toffoli depth can be reduced to one. We also present space-depth tradeoffs and an application to programmable rotations.

AI.tldr: Reversible in-place quantum addition modulo $2^n-1$ can be done in constant Toffoli depth with $O(n)$ space under a non-standard encoding, and reduced to Toffoli depth one via measurement-based uncomputation, with space-depth tradeoffs and an application to programmable rotations.
AI.motivation: Standard reversible/quantum adders exhibit circuit depth growing with the word size, which is a bottleneck for fault-tolerant quantum arithmetic. The authors seek constant-depth, in-place addition modulo $2^n-1$ without excessive auxiliary space.
AI.method: The construction exploits a non-standard encoding of the variables to enable in-place, reversible addition modulo $2^n-1$ using $O(n)$ space in constant Toffoli depth. Measurement-based uncomputation is then applied to further compress the Toffoli depth down to one, and a family of space-depth tradeoff circuits is derived.
AI.result: Addition modulo $2^n-1$ is achieved in constant Toffoli depth with $O(n)$ space, and in Toffoli depth one using measurement-based uncomputation. Space-depth tradeoffs are characterized, and the construction yields an efficient programmable-rotation primitive.
AI.conclusion: Encoding choice and measurement-based uncomputation are powerful levers for depth-optimal quantum arithmetic; the approach gives constant (even unit) Toffoli depth modular addition and supports applications such as programmable rotations.

title: Quantum query complexity of Hurwitz stability testing
summary: Determining whether every trajectory of the linear system $\dot{x}=Ax$ converges to zero (or, equivalently, whether $A$ is Hurwitz stable) is a fundamental problem in control theory. It arises, for example, in verifying the stability of feedback controllers and state observers, as well as of linearized dynamical models. We study the quantum query complexity of deciding whether a matrix $A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ is Hurwitz stable, given an exact normalized block-encoding of $A$. The query complexity is characterized in terms of the system dimension $n$ and a supplied lower bound $0<ν\leq ω_A$ on the imaginary-axis distance $ω_A:=\min_{t\in\mathbb{R}}σ_{\min}(A-\mathrm{i}tI)$, where $σ_{\min}(A)$ is the smallest singular value of $A$. We prove a query-complexity lower bound of $Ω(\sqrt{n}/ν)$, which holds even when $A$ is restricted to be real and diagonal. For general matrices with nonzero $ω_A$, we encode an approximation of the right-half-plane spectral projector $\operatorname{sign}^+(A):=(I+\operatorname{sign}(A))/2$ as a block of a matrix inverse, where $A$ is Hurwitz if and only if the projector is zero. To test this, we produce a quantum algorithm which determines if a $(β,b,1/(4\sqrt{n}))$-block-encoded projector matrix (like $\operatorname{sign}^+(A)$) is zero or not; for constant success probability, it has complexity $Θ(β\sqrt{n})$. When the zero test is applied to specific approximations of $\operatorname{sign}^+(A)$, this yields an upper bound of $O(\sqrt{n}ν^{-2}\log(\sqrt{n}/ν))$ queries in the general case, and $O(\sqrt{n}ν^{-1}\log n)$ when $A$ is Hermitian or normal. The latter upper bound matches the lower bound up to a logarithmic factor. Thus the dimension dependence of quantum Hurwitz testing is nearly optimal, while the remaining factor in the non-normal case isolates an open conditioning gap.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes the quantum query complexity of deciding whether a matrix A is Hurwitz stable given a block-encoding, proving a lower bound of Ω(√n/ν) and an upper bound of O(√n ν⁻² log(√n/ν)) in general (tight up to log for Hermitian/normal matrices).
AI.motivation: Hurwitz stability of ẋ=Ax is fundamental in control theory, arising in verifying stability of feedback controllers, observers, and linearized models. The authors aim to establish the quantum query complexity of this decision problem in terms of dimension n and the imaginary-axis distance ω_A.
AI.method: A lower bound of Ω(√n/ν) is proved (even for real diagonal A). For the upper bound, the right-half-plane spectral projector sign⁺(A)=(I+sign(A))/2 is encoded as a block of a matrix inverse, with A Hurwitz iff this projector is zero. A quantum zero-test for (β,b,1/(4√n))-block-encoded projectors is designed with complexity Θ(β√n), then applied to specific approximations of sign⁺(A).
AI.result: A query lower bound of Ω(√n/ν) and an upper bound of O(√n ν⁻² log(√n/ν)) for general matrices, improving to O(√n ν⁻¹ log n) when A is Hermitian or normal—matching the lower bound up to a logarithmic factor.
AI.conclusion: The dimension dependence of quantum Hurwitz testing is nearly optimal, and for Hermitian/normal matrices the complexity is essentially tight. The remaining ν factor in the non-normal case identifies an open conditioning gap.

title: Anomalous superradiant phases in a quantum Rabi zigzag chain under a synthetic gauge field
summary: We present the phase diagram of a one-dimensional quantum Rabi zigzag chain under an artificial gauge field, which is implemented via phase-modulated next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) hopping. For a system size of $N=8$, we analytically determine the order parameters and critical thresholds, identifying five distinct superradiant phases. For strong nearest-neighbor (NN) coupling, the system exhibits either a ferro-superradiant (FSR) or an antiferro-superradiant (AFSR) phase depending on its sign. Increasing NNN coupling induces a stripe antiferro-superradiant (sAFSR) phase with antiparallel NNN and parallel NN displacements, which is distinct from the conventional AFSR phase. Tuning the magnetic flux drives the system into chiral or antichiral superradiant phases with opposite ground-state photon currents, which are different from the conventional superradiant phases. Remarkably, geometric frustration within each triangular plaquette stabilizes chiral phases even at small magnetic flux while suppressing the sAFSR phase, which vanishes for $N=6$. Mapping the system onto an effective magnetic Hamiltonian yields an analogous phase diagram featuring distinct magnetic phases, offering insight into the anomalous superradiant phases. This equivalence establishes a quantum optical platform for simulating chiral magnetism.

AI.tldr: A phase diagram of a 1D quantum Rabi zigzag chain under an artificial gauge field (phase-modulated NNN hopping) is derived analytically for N=8, revealing five distinct superradiant phases—FSR/AFSR, stripe AFSR (sAFSR), and chiral/antichiral phases—with geometric frustration stabilizing chiral photon currents and an exact mapping to an effective magnetic Hamiltonian.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to explore how an artificial gauge field combined with zigzag geometry and competing NN/NNN couplings enriches the superradiant phase structure of the quantum Rabi chain, and to establish a quantum optical analogue of frustrated chiral magnetism.
