AI.method: Analytical treatment of a one-dimensional quantum Rabi zigzag chain of size N=8 with phase-modulated NNN hopping generating an artificial magnetic flux. Order parameters and critical thresholds are determined analytically, and the system is mapped onto an effective magnetic Hamiltonian whose phase diagram is analyzed by analogy.
AI.result: Five superradiant phases are identified: ferro-superradiant (FSR) and antiferro-superradiant (AFSR) set by the sign of strong NN coupling; a stripe AFSR (sAFSR) phase with antiparallel NNN and parallel NN displacements; and chiral/antichiral phases with opposite ground-state photon currents. Geometric frustration within triangular plaquettes stabilizes the chiral phases at small flux, suppresses sAFSR, and the sAFSR phase disappears for N=6. The effective magnetic Hamiltonian reproduces an analogous phase diagram with distinct magnetic phases.
AI.conclusion: Artificial gauge fields in a zigzag Rabi chain generate anomalous superradiant phases governed by geometric frustration, and the equivalence to an effective magnetic Hamiltonian establishes a quantum optical platform for simulating chiral magnetism.

title: Biorthogonal universal quantum control
summary: As a paradigm for describing open-quantum-system dynamics, the non-Hermitian Schrödinger equation generally modifies state norms, complicating coherent control over the system's Hilbert space. With a general instantaneous frame spanned by biorthogonal ancillary bases, we develop a biorthogonal quantum-control theory for discrete-variable systems governed by time-dependent non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. In particular, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for extracting the transitionless pathways that transport parallel in ket and bra states. When this condition is satisfied by a set of projectors constructed with biorthogonal basis states, the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian becomes diagonal in the relevant biorthogonal subspace, enabling arbitrary initial state to evolve as a superposition of controlled transitionless passages. We further identify the parametric constraints under which the transformation linking the initial and final states becomes unitary. As a result, the final system state is automatically normalized even though the transitional dynamics is nonunitary. Our theory is justified by the bidirectional population transfer and a holomonic quantum gate implemented by a non-Hermitian three-level system in $Λ$ type. For the population transfer, controlled gain and loss reduce the required coherent pulse area, enabling shorter transfer times than the Hermitian benchmark with the same average Rabi frequency. Our work integrates the universal quantum control (UQC) into the biorthogonal representation, displaying full-rank passage engineering with coherent operations in non-Hermitian systems.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a biorthogonal quantum-control theory for discrete-variable systems under time-dependent non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, deriving a necessary and sufficient condition for transitionless (shortcut-to-adiabaticity-like) passages and identifying when initial-to-final transformations become unitary; the framework is validated by bidirectional population transfer and a holonomic gate in a non-Hermitian Λ-type three-level system.
AI.motivation: The non-Hermitian Schrödinger equation alters state norms, which complicates coherent control over Hilbert space. Existing quantum-control paradigms are largely built in the Hermitian/orthonormal setting, so a control theory adapted to biorthogonal bases is needed to engineer passages in non-Hermitian systems.
AI.method: Introduce a general instantaneous frame spanned by biorthogonal ancillary bases and formulate biorthogonal quantum control for time-dependent non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. Derive a necessary and sufficient condition for extracting transitionless pathways transporting parallel ket and bra states. Construct projectors from biorthogonal basis states so the Hamiltonian is diagonal in the relevant biorthogonal subspace, allowing arbitrary initial states to evolve as superpositions of controlled transitionless passages. Then identify parametric constraints under which the initial-to-final transformation is unitary despite nonunitary intermediate dynamics (auto-normalized final state). Apply the theory to bidirectional population transfer and a holonomic quantum gate in a non-Hermitian Λ-type three-level system.
AI.result: A necessary and sufficient condition for transitionless passages is obtained, together with the diagonalization of the Hamiltonian in the biorthogonal subspace and the parametric conditions for a unitary initial-to-final map (final state automatically normalized). Controlled gain and loss reduce the required coherent pulse area for population transfer, giving shorter transfer times than the Hermitian benchmark at equal average Rabi frequency; a holonomic quantum gate is realized in the non-Hermitian Λ system.
AI.conclusion: The work integrates universal quantum control into the biorthogonal representation, demonstrating full-rank passage engineering with coherent operations in non-Hermitian systems, with practical advantages (reduced pulse area, faster transfer) and a route to non-Hermitian holonomic gates.

title: Quantum Advantage in Beam-Displacement Estimation for Inter-Satellite Quantum-Secure Time Transfer
summary: In this work, we investigate the practical feasibility of achieving a quantum advantage, in the context of inter-satellite quantum communication, of satellite position estimation. The investigation focuses on a quantum-enhanced scheme in which squeezing is added to the derivative mode of a Gaussian probe beam as a means of estimating photon-beam displacement. The performance of the scheme is compared against the standard quantum limit achieved by an optimal classical beam-displacement estimation scheme under a fair same-total-energy constraint. We find that although the benefit provided by squeezing rapidly diminishes as the inter-satellite distance increases due to diffraction-induced beam spreading and subsequent truncation by the finite receiver aperture, a quantum advantage can still be expected over inter-satellite distances up to approximately 100 km under practical satellite configurations. This distance scale between satellites is anticipated for Starlink-type satellite constellations.

AI.tldr: The paper assesses whether squeezing the derivative mode of a Gaussian probe beam yields a practical quantum advantage for inter-satellite satellite-position estimation, and finds an advantage surviving up to ~100 km ranges under realistic satellite configurations.
AI.motivation: Satellite position estimation via photon-beam displacement is fundamentally limited, and while quantum-enhanced (squeezed) probes are known to beat the standard quantum limit, their practical value under realistic inter-satellite conditions—diffraction spreading and finite receiver apertures—had not been established. Starlink-type constellations operating at ~100 km inter-satellite separations motivate this feasibility assessment.
AI.method: A quantum-enhanced Gaussian probe beam with squeezing added to the derivative mode is used to estimate photon-beam displacement. Performance is benchmarked against the standard quantum limit attained by an optimal classical beam-displacement estimation scheme, under a fair same-total-energy constraint. The model incorporates diffraction-induced beam spreading over propagation and truncation by the finite receiver aperture.
AI.result: The squeezing benefit degrades rapidly with increasing inter-satellite distance, owing to diffraction spreading and subsequent aperture truncation. Nevertheless, a quantum advantage over the optimal classical scheme persists at ranges up to approximately 100 km under practical satellite configurations.
AI.conclusion: Quantum advantage for inter-satellite satellite position estimation is practically feasible at distance scales relevant to Starlink-type constellations (~100 km), despite the erosion of squeezing gain from diffraction and finite-aperture truncation.

title: Testing hardware quantum machine learning claims with a null circuit: fill prediction on Binance futures with 129 qubits of an IBM Heron processor
summary: Quantum processors are now used as feature generators for classical models on tabular data. A circuit encodes each record, the device returns expectation values, and a classical model learns from them. A recent report claimed large gains from such features, gains that appeared only on noisy hardware. These claims are hard to check, because a quantum device is not a static function. Its state changes from job to job and from one calibration to the next, and that drift can leak information about the outcome into the features. We propose a five-step protocol for testing claims of this kind. It runs a circuit that carries no data in the same jobs as the real one. It checks whether the hardware leaves a recognizable mark on each job. It compares random and natural assignments of records to jobs, replays the null results under other submission orders, and closes the leak with a job-purged backtest. We apply it, pre-registered, to the HSBC and IBM study of fill probabilities in bond trading, which reported a large hardware-only gain. We use a public analog task and run the study's circuit on a 129-qubit chain of an IBM Heron processor. Under controlled assignment the hardware features give no gain over classical features, and the device reproduces the ideal features about as well as shot noise allows. Yet every job carries a distinct fingerprint. A circuit with no data at all predicts fills well above chance when records are batched by outcome and the same job sits on both sides of the train/test split. Removing that overlap removes the effect. The protocol costs under an hour of processor time and is designed for any hardware feature or kernel pipeline on tabular data.

AI.tldr: A pre-registered five-step protocol shows that a reported hardware-only quantum advantage in tabular features (bond fill probabilities) is an artifact of job-level hardware drift leaking outcome information; with controlled job assignment, quantum features give no gain over classical ones, and the effect vanishes once job overlap between train and test is removed.
AI.motivation: Quantum processors are increasingly used as feature generators for classical models on tabular data, and a recent study (HSBC/IBM on bond-trading fill probabilities) claimed large gains that appeared only on noisy hardware. Such claims are hard to verify because quantum devices are not static functions: their state drifts from job to job and across calibrations, potentially leaking outcome-related information into the features. The authors aim to provide a rigorous, reproducible way to test these claims.
AI.method: A five-step auditing protocol: (1) run a data-free (null) circuit in the same jobs as the real circuit; (2) check whether the hardware leaves a recognizable per-job fingerprint; (3) compare random versus natural assignments of records to jobs; (4) replay null results under alternative submission orders; and (5) close the leak with a job-purged backtest that removes train/test job overlap. Applied pre-registered to the HSBC/IBM study using a public analog task on the study's circuit executed on a 129-qubit IBM Heron processor chain.
AI.result: Under controlled assignment, hardware features yield no gain over classical features, and the device reproduces ideal features about as well as shot noise permits. However, every job carries a distinct fingerprint. A data-free circuit predicts fills well above chance when records are batched by outcome and the same job sits on both sides of the train/test split. Removing that job overlap eliminates the effect.
AI.conclusion: The reported hardware-only gain is an artifact of job-level device drift rather than a genuine quantum feature advantage. The protocol requires under an hour of processor time and generalizes to any hardware feature or kernel pipeline on tabular data.

title: Parametric Enhancement of an Optical Spring in a Dark Signal-Recycling Cavity
summary: Optical springs tailor the response of precision sensors. Parametric amplification of the signal field stiffens the spring, extending the precision to higher frequencies. A Michelson interferometer operated at a dark fringe is the most direct way to separate the signal from the carrier for amplification. We experimentally demonstrate such quantum manipulation of the optical spring by placing an optical parametric amplifier in a cavity at the dark port, showing a significant increase of the optical-spring constant with the parametric gain within a factor of four below the oscillation threshold.

AI.tldr: The authors experimentally realize quantum manipulation of an optical spring by placing an optical parametric amplifier (OPA) at the dark port of a dark-fringe Michelson interferometer, achieving a significant gain-dependent stiffening of the optical-spring constant.
AI.motivation: Optical springs determine the response of precision sensors; parametric amplification can stiffen the spring to extend measurement precision to higher frequencies, but a clean way to separate the signal field from the carrier for amplification was needed.
AI.method: A Michelson interferometer is operated at a dark fringe to isolate the signal from the carrier, and an optical parametric amplifier housed in a cavity is placed at the dark-port output so the signal field is parametrically amplified; the optical-spring constant is measured as a function of parametric gain up to four times below the oscillation threshold.
AI.result: The optical-spring constant increases significantly with parametric gain, reaching roughly a factor-of-four enhancement while remaining below the oscillation threshold.
AI.conclusion: Quantum manipulation of the optical spring via dark-port parametric amplification is experimentally feasible and offers a route to stiffened springs and extended high-frequency precision in optical sensors.

title: Estimation of Quantum Umlaut Information
summary: Quantifying correlations is important for understanding how quantum states and channels support information processing. Quantum umlaut information $U$ connects such correlations to reliability in hypothesis testing and certain communication settings, but its known formulas require classical descriptions of the underlying states. To estimate correlations without these descriptions, we introduce measured quantum umlaut information $U^M$ by replacing Umegaki relative entropy with measured relative entropy. Its variational formulation leads to a quantum generative adversarial framework for estimating $U^M$ from measurement statistics of unknown bipartite states and classical-quantum channels. This framework optimizes reference states and measurements without reconstructing the target states or channel outputs. For classical-quantum channels, it also optimizes the input probabilities. We further analyze the relation between $U^M$ and $U$, deriving a state-dependent gap bound and characterizing equality for full-rank bipartite states. Numerical simulations show trained estimates close on average to independently computed numerical references for $U^M$ across the tested states and channels. These estimates could help assess how well quantum memories preserve correlations and how noise or drift affects input-output dependence in quantum transmitters and state-preparation devices.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces measured quantum umlaut information $U^M$, obtained by replacing Umegaki relative entropy with measured relative entropy, to estimate quantum correlations without classical descriptions of states. A variational formulation yields a quantum generative adversarial framework that estimates $U^M$ from measurement statistics of unknown bipartite states and classical-quantum channels, with a state-dependent gap bound to $U$ and numerical validation.
AI.motivation: Quantum umlaut information $U$ links correlations to reliability in hypothesis testing and communication, but its known formulas require classical descriptions of the underlying states, preventing estimation from measurement data alone for unknown states and channels.
AI.method: Define measured quantum umlaut information $U^M$ by substituting Umegaki relative entropy with measured relative entropy. Derive a variational formulation leading to a quantum generative adversarial framework that jointly optimizes reference states and measurements (and input probabilities for classical-quantum channels) without reconstructing target states or channel outputs. Analyze the $U^M$–$U$ relation, deriving a state-dependent gap bound and equality conditions for full-rank bipartite states.
AI.result: A state-dependent gap bound between $U^M$ and $U$ is established, with equality characterized for full-rank bipartite states. Numerical simulations show trained estimates closely match independently computed numerical references for $U^M$ across tested states and channels.
AI.conclusion: $U^M$ enables description-free estimation of quantum correlations from measurement statistics via an adversarial optimization framework, with controlled deviation from $U$. The estimates can support assessing how well quantum memories preserve correlations and how noise or drift affects input-output dependence in quantum transmitters and state-preparation devices.

title: Optimality of the Petz-Fuchs Smoothed State
summary: Quantum state smoothing is an estimation technique that uses past and future measurement information obtained from a continuous-in-time measurement record to reconstruct the state of an open quantum system. Recently, there has been a new approach to quantum state smoothing based on quantum retrodiction known as the Petz-Fuchs smoothed state. Here I prove that this Petz-Fuchs smoothed state majorizes all other smoothed states that only depend on the filtered state (the operator conditioned on the past measurement record) and the retrofiltered effect (the operator describing the future measurement record). To do this, I characterize the set of all possible smoothed states satisfying this condition.

AI.tldr: The Petz-Fuchs smoothed quantum state majorizes every other smoothed state that depends only on the filtered state and retrofiltered effect.
AI.motivation: Quantum state smoothing reconstructs an open quantum system's state using both past and future information from a continuous measurement record. The recently introduced Petz-Fuchs smoothed state (based on quantum retrodiction) lacks a comparative characterization against alternative smoothing schemes.
AI.method: The author characterizes the full set of smoothed states that depend only on the filtered state (operator conditioned on past records) and the retrofiltered effect (operator describing the future record), then proves a majorization relation for the Petz-Fuchs state within this set.
AI.result: The Petz-Fuchs smoothed state is shown to majorize all other smoothed states constructed solely from the filtered state and retrofiltered effect.
AI.conclusion: The Petz-Fuchs smoothed state occupies an extremal position in the space of smoothed states, providing a rigorous ordering (in the majorization sense) among smoothing approaches based on past-filtered and future-retrofiltered information.

title: PyQLAS: A Quantum-Classical Hybrid Solver Library for Linear Systems
summary: Quantum algorithms solve a linear system at a cost that grows only polylogarithmically in its dimension, but on present-day hardware that advantage is realised only if the quantum and the classical parts of a solve are apportioned deliberately. We present PyQLAS, a quantum--classical hybrid library for linear systems that exposes this apportionment as a design parameter rather than a fixed assumption. PyQLAS builds three nested solvers around a single variational core---a variational solver, an outer residual iteration, and a Krylov-subspace projection---so that the quantum subroutine can be held at a fixed circuit width while the classical host absorbs the growth of the problem. Around them, the library supplies preconditioning at two independent levels, dimension alignment, checkpointing, and device-budget control, and a solve written against the interface runs unchanged on an exact state-vector simulator, on a local sampler, and on a real superconducting processor. The library is validated on the IEEE 118-bus power flow, a standard test system in which the linear solver is embedded in a classical Newton iteration. There, the iteration converges to the specified tolerance and reproduces the classical reference solution to within $2.3\times10^{-8}$ p.u.\ in voltage magnitude and $3.4\times10^{-6}$ degrees in voltage angle.

AI.tldr: PyQLAS is a quantum–classical hybrid library for linear systems that treats the split of work between the quantum subroutine and the classical host as an explicit design parameter, offering three nested solvers around one variational core and validated on the IEEE 118-bus power flow.
AI.motivation: Quantum linear-system algorithms scale polylogarithmically in dimension, but this advantage is only realisable on current hardware if quantum and classical work are deliberately apportioned; existing approaches fix this apportionment rather than expose it as a tunable design choice.
AI.method: PyQLAS builds three nested solvers around a single variational core—a variational solver, an outer residual iteration, and a Krylov-subspace projection—so the quantum subroutine stays at fixed circuit width while the classical host absorbs problem growth. The library adds two independent levels of preconditioning, dimension alignment, checkpointing, and device-budget control, with a device-agnostic interface spanning an exact state-vector simulator, a local sampler, and a real superconducting processor.
AI.result: Validated on the IEEE 118-bus power flow embedded in a classical Newton iteration, the solve converges to the specified tolerance and reproduces the classical reference to within 2.3e-8 p.u. in voltage magnitude and 3.4e-6 degrees in voltage angle.
AI.conclusion: Deliberate apportionment of quantum versus classical work enables practical hybrid linear solvers at fixed circuit width, and PyQLAS demonstrates this portability across simulators and real quantum hardware while matching classical accuracy on a standard power-system benchmark.

title: Time-Domain Multiplexing for Resource-Efficient Heralded GKP State Preparation
summary: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are key resources for fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, but their conditional preparation via Gaussian boson sampling involves a trade-off between source count and photon-number resolution. Distributing heralding photons across more measured modes reduces the resolution required per mode, yet increases the number of simultaneously operated squeezed sources in fully squeezed spatial architectures. Here, we show that time-domain multiplexing (TDM) can reduce these physical source requirements while preserving GKP state quality. Using an end-to-end differentiable Bargmann framework, we find that TDM circuits reusing one or two squeezed sources achieve fidelities comparable to fully squeezed spatial circuits across several configurations. Selected nine-mode configurations retain fidelities above 0.95 with one photon heralded in each measured mode, mitigating detector resolution demands without a proportional increase in source count. Loss-aware reoptimization further shows that, under the investigated spatial loss models, two-mode TDM maintains fidelities near 0.80 at 1.0 dB per channel, whereas the corresponding spatial benchmarks fall below 0.60. These results demonstrate that temporal reuse provides an effective architectural route for balancing source overhead, detection demands, and state preparation performance in the presence of optical loss.

AI.tldr: Time-domain multiplexing (TDM) reusing one or two squeezed sources can prepare GKP states with fidelities comparable to fully squeezed spatial circuits, easing the source-count versus photon-number-resolution trade-off in Gaussian boson sampling, and it is more robust to optical loss.
AI.motivation: Conditional GKP state preparation via Gaussian boson sampling faces an inherent trade-off: spreading heralding photons over more measured modes lowers required photon-number resolution per mode, but in fully squeezed spatial architectures it demands proportionally more simultaneously operated squeezed sources.
AI.method: The authors use an end-to-end differentiable Bargmann framework to simulate and optimize GKP state preparation circuits, comparing TDM circuits that reuse one or two squeezed sources against fully squeezed spatial benchmarks, including loss-aware reoptimization.
AI.result: TDM circuits match fully squeezed spatial circuits across several configurations; selected nine-mode configurations retain fidelities above 0.95 with one photon heralded per measured mode. Under the investigated spatial loss models at 1.0 dB per channel, two-mode TDM keeps fidelity near 0.80 while spatial benchmarks fall below 0.60.
AI.conclusion: Temporal reuse of squeezed sources is an effective architectural route for balancing source overhead, detection resolution demands, and GKP state preparation quality, particularly under optical loss.

title: Loss-aware optimization of realistic GKP gid states
summary: Realistic preparation of Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states, the prime candidates for quantum computation with bosonic systems, is inevitably burdened by photon loss. We show how taking this loss into account can lead to more robust quantum states, thereby diminishing its negative influence. Using GKP squeezing as an operational figure of merit, we formulate a loss-aware optimization procedure based on the ground state representation of GKP states. Numerical simulations for square, hexagonal, and asymmetric GKP states show that the optimal preparation generally requires a different initial grid spacing than that of the desired ideal code state. For symmetric and hexagonal lattices, the optimal parameters asymptotically follow the simple scaling relation. The optimized states exhibit better GKP squeezing and greater resilience to losses. These results provide a simple and experimentally relevant strategy for improving realistic photonic GKP state preparation in the presence of known photon loss.

AI.tldr: Loss-aware optimization of GKP state preparation, based on the ground-state representation, improves GKP squeezing and resilience to photon loss; the optimal initial grid spacing generally differs from the ideal code state's.
AI.motivation: Realistic preparation of GKP states, the leading candidates for bosonic quantum computation, is inevitably degraded by photon loss. The authors aim to turn this unavoidable loss into a design consideration so that the resulting states are more robust rather than merely degraded.
AI.method: Using GKP squeezing as an operational figure of merit, the authors formulate a loss-aware optimization procedure grounded in the ground-state representation of GKP states, and apply it numerically to square, hexagonal, and asymmetric GKP states.
AI.result: Simulations show the optimal preparation generally requires an initial grid spacing different from that of the desired ideal code state. For symmetric and hexagonal lattices, the optimal parameters asymptotically follow a simple scaling relation. Optimized states yield better GKP squeezing and greater resilience to loss.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for known photon loss in the preparation stage gives a simple, experimentally relevant strategy for improving realistic photonic GKP state preparation.

title: Helper-assisted quantum sensing with low dressed-state leakage
comment: 31 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23796406
summary: We study a two-qubit sensing protocol in which only a helper qubit is read out. Calibrated loading and unloading encode a transverse signal in the helper's phase, keep leakage out of a selected dressed-state band small, and return the sensor close to its idle ground state. We derive an information bound for a single sensor whose excitation stays below a prescribed budget, and simulate repeated operation with an uncertain coupling and finite-duration resets in a driven open-system model. At the tested settings, finite measurement records support estimation with infrequent resets. A helper flip at zero coupling, combined with a reversal of the coupling sign, suppresses a static helper offset shared across a record while retaining the signal, at a cost of about 27% of the no-offset information of a plain sequence of equal duration. Under slowly varying noise, averaging each cycle's likelihood over the correct noise law removes most of the added bias, and a wrong noise law can worsen the estimate. A selected directly read sensor with ideal controls and repeated nondemolition verification has the higher information rate. Any practical benefit of avoiding direct readout therefore requires a device-specific disturbance model.

AI.tldr: A two-qubit sensing scheme where only a helper qubit is read out is analyzed, with calibrated load/unload encoding a transverse signal in the helper's phase; an information bound, open-system simulations, and offset-suppression via helper flip plus coupling-sign reversal are derived.
AI.motivation: Direct readout of the sensor qubit may disturb it; the paper asks whether reading out only a helper qubit can outperform a directly read sensor, and under what device-specific conditions such avoidance of direct readout yields practical benefit.
AI.method: Calibrated loading/unloading protocol to encode a transverse signal in the helper's phase while suppressing leakage out of a selected dressed-state band and restoring the sensor near its idle ground state; derivation of an information bound for a single sensor with bounded excitation; driven open-system simulations with uncertain coupling and finite-duration resets; a helper-flip-at-zero-coupling plus coupling-sign-reversal sequence to cancel a static helper offset; likelihood averaging over the noise law under slowly varying noise.
AI.result: Finite measurement records permit estimation with infrequent resets at tested settings. The flip-and-reversal offset-suppression retains the signal while costing about 27% of the no-offset information of an equal-duration plain sequence. Averaging each cycle's likelihood over the correct noise law removes most added bias, whereas a wrong noise law can worsen the estimate. A directly read sensor with ideal controls and repeated nondemolition verification achieves the higher information rate.
AI.conclusion: Avoiding direct readout offers no intrinsic information advantage; any practical benefit requires a device-specific disturbance model justifying the helper-readout overhead.

title: Real-time BP decoding of a high-rate QEC code
summary: We present a real-time FPGA decoder for a high-rate $[[512,174,8]]$ 3D product qLDPC code. We construct a circuit-level detector-error model for a compact syndrome-extraction schedule and propose a small parallel ensemble of row-wise serial min-sum decoders with cumulative memory. The decoder matches $\text{BP+OSD-CS}_\text{10}$ accuracy with one core and Relay-BP accuracy with three cores. The FPGA implementation meets the latency budget of neutral-atom and trapped-ion systems. An ASIC implementation would improve the latency, enabling real time decoding even for superconducting systems. At a physical error rate of $p=10^{-3}$, three FPGA devices decode 174 logical qubits with a logical error rate of $5\times10^{-7}$ and effective distance 6. For $p=10^{-4}$, and assuming the number of BP iterations is capped to 30, the decoder's average latency is $5.1\,$\textmu s and its worst-case latency is $97.9\,$\textmu s.

AI.tldr: A real-time FPGA decoder for a high-rate [[512,174,8]] 3D product qLDPC code, using parallel row-wise serial min-sum cores with cumulative memory, achieves BP+OSD-CS_10 and Relay-BP accuracy and meets neutral-atom/trapped-ion latency budgets.
AI.motivation: Quantum LDPC codes promise high encoding rates, but practical deployment requires a decoder that simultaneously achieves high accuracy and real-time low latency compatible with physical qubit platforms.
AI.method: The authors build a circuit-level detector-error model for a compact syndrome-extraction schedule, and design a small parallel ensemble of row-wise serial min-sum decoders with cumulative memory, implemented on FPGA.
AI.result: One core matches BP+OSD-CS_10 accuracy; three cores match Relay-BP accuracy. At p=10^-3, three FPGAs decode 174 logical qubits with LER 5e-7 and effective distance 6. At p=10^-4 with BP iterations capped at 30, average latency is 5.1 µs and worst-case 97.9 µs. The design meets neutral-atom and trapped-ion latency budgets; an ASIC would enable real-time decoding for superconducting systems.
AI.conclusion: The FPGA decoder provides accurate, real-time-compatible decoding of a high-rate qLDPC code, with ASIC scaling identified as a path to superconducting-system real-time operation.

title: Analytic level statistics of the quantum Rabi model
summary: We derive an analytic expression for the distribution of level spacings in the quantum Rabi model. At high energies, the spectrum in a fixed parity sector takes the asymptotic form of a uniformly spaced ladder modulated by a decaying oscillation. The alternating sign of this oscillation separates successive spacings into two branches. For a finite window containing many oscillations, counting how often the two branches exceed a given spacing yields an analytic expression for the spacing density at leading order. The oscillation amplitude at the lower end of the window sets the range of spacings, and its value at the upper end fixes the positions of two cusps that form twin peaks. Spacing histograms from exact diagonalization agree with the analytic density, including its spacing range and twin peak positions. At leading order, the same spectral analysis also yields an expression for the ratio of consecutive spacings, a statistic that requires no spectral unfolding. The resulting ratio statistics agree closely with those from exact diagonalization. For windows that continue to contain many oscillations, the spacing and ratio peaks move toward unity at higher energies as the spectrum approaches a uniformly spaced ladder. The same counting approach can be explored in other systems with controlled spectral asymptotics, slowly varying spacing branches, and windows containing many oscillations.

AI.tldr: Analytic asymptotic expression is derived for the level-spacing distribution (and consecutive-spacing ratio) of the quantum Rabi model, showing a twin-peaked structure whose range and peak positions are set by the oscillation amplitude of the spectrum's ladder-like asymptotic form, validated against exact diagonalization.
AI.motivation: The quantum Rabi model lacks a closed-form characterization of its spectral statistics, particularly spacing distributions that go beyond Wigner–Dyson or Poisson universality; an analytic handle on its level statistics is desirable.
AI.method: Start from the asymptotic spectrum in a fixed parity sector, which is a uniformly spaced ladder modulated by a decaying oscillation whose alternating sign splits spacings into two slowly varying branches. Counting, over a window containing many oscillations, the fraction of each branch exceeding a given spacing gives the spacing density at leading order; the lower-end oscillation amplitude fixes the spacing range and the upper-end value fixes two cusps forming twin peaks. The same counting yields a consecutive-spacing-ratio statistic requiring no unfolding.
AI.result: The analytic spacing density reproduces exact-diagonalization histograms, including the bounded spacing range and the twin-peak positions; the analytic ratio distribution agrees closely with numerics. For windows still containing many oscillations, spacing and ratio peaks migrate toward unity at higher energy as the spectrum approaches a uniform ladder.
AI.conclusion: The spectral asymptotics of the Rabi model admit a controlled counting analysis that yields analytic level statistics; the approach generalizes to other systems with slowly varying spacing branches, controlled asymptotics, and oscillatory windows dense enough for the counting approximation.

title: oracq: A Modular Framework for Implementing and Analyzing Quantum Scientific Computing Algorithms
summary: Quantum algorithms for scientific computing are specified against access models such as block-encodings, sparse oracles, state preparations, and quantum random-access memories. Their concrete realization is deliberately left open, yet it is a research variable that changes both the numerical behavior and the resource cost of the program, so every reported conclusion is attributable to one realization. In this paper, we present oracq, a Python framework that makes this choice a managed and checkable decision. Our claim is linguistic rather than infrastructural. Algorithms are stored as persistent register-level programs whose oracle slots are declared and typed but unimplemented. A separate binding pass links compatible realizations, so one stored algorithm can be re-bound to a gate network, a QRAM-backed table, or compiled reversible arithmetic and compared across them. Typed QRAM resources, a compiler from pure Python numerical formulas to reversible fixed-point circuits, and block-encoding algebra with qubitization and QSVT-style kernels supply the constructions. Two end-to-end workflows exercise the framework, a quantum finite-volume pipeline for the compressible Euler equations and a quantum homotopy-analysis pipeline that lifts nonlinear PDEs to composable linear input models. The verification methodology separates implementation error from method error, and logical resource accounts cover programs before and after binding. The framework is openly available at https://github.com/IAI-USTC-Quantum/oracq.

AI.tldr: oracq is a Python framework that stores quantum scientific-computing algorithms as register-level programs with declared but unimplemented oracle slots, then re-binds those slots to different access realizations (gate networks, QRAM tables, compiled reversible arithmetic) so numerical behavior and resource costs become explicit, checkable decisions.
AI.motivation: Quantum algorithms for scientific computing are specified against access models (block-encodings, sparse oracles, state preparations, QRAM) whose concrete realization is left open. Because the realization changes both numerics and resource cost, every reported conclusion is attributable to a particular realization; the authors want this choice to be managed and checkable rather than implicit.
AI.method: The framework stores algorithms as persistent register-level programs whose oracle slots are declared and typed but unimplemented; a separate binding pass links compatible realizations so one stored algorithm can be re-bound to a gate network, a QRAM-backed table, or compiled reversible arithmetic. Constructions include typed QRAM resources, a compiler from pure Python numerical formulas to reversible fixed-point circuits, and block-encoding algebra with qubitization and QSVT-style kernels. Verification separates implementation error from method error, and logical resource accounts cover programs before and after binding.
AI.result: Two end-to-end workflows are exercised: a quantum finite-volume pipeline for the compressible Euler equations, and a quantum homotopy-analysis pipeline that lifts nonlinear PDEs to composable linear input models. The framework enables cross-realization comparison of a single stored algorithm and provides pre- and post-binding logical resource accounts.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is linguistic rather than infrastructural: access-model realization becomes a first-class, typed, re-bindable decision in the program representation, with verification and resource accounting made explicit. The framework is openly available at https://github.com/IAI-USTC-Quantum/oracq.

title: Almost-Quantum Correlations Violate Information Causality
comment: 4.5 pages, two-column, 1 figure; comments are welcome
summary: Information causality (IC) posits that communicating m classical bits cannot give the receiver access to more than m bits of information about the sender's independent data. Although IC holds in quantum theory and excludes a broad class of supra-quantum correlations, its validity for the almost-quantum set has remained open. This semidefinite relaxation of the quantum set satisfies nontrivial communication complexity, no advantage for non-local computation, macroscopic locality, local orthogonality, and numerical evidence has suggested that it may also satisfy IC. Here we show that almost-quantum correlations violate IC, and do so without bound. Unlike earlier violations of IC, which rely on biased guesses, ours is driven by zero-error certificates: each is rare but never wrong, carries information linear in its probability, and vouches for many of the sender's bits at once. This establishes a sharp dichotomy: either IC is a valid physical principle that excludes these correlations, or any nonsignalling theory realizing them admits no mutual information obeying consistency, data processing and the chain rule. In the latter case, we discuss why the chain rule is the natural property to relinquish, and how this possibility relates to histories-based formulations and to locality defined relative to the state rather than presupposed in a fixed spacetime.

AI.tldr: Almost-quantum correlations violate information causality without bound, via zero-error certificates rather than biased guesses.
AI.motivation: Information causality (IC) excludes many supra-quantum correlations and holds in quantum theory, but its validity for the almost-quantum set—a semidefinite relaxation satisfying several other physical principles—was open despite numerical hints. The authors aim to settle this question.
AI.method: Construct almost-quantum correlations that violate IC and analyze the violation mechanism, characterizing it as driven by zero-error certificates (rare but never incorrect, each carrying information linear in its probability and certifying many of the sender's bits simultaneously).
AI.result: Almost-quantum correlations violate IC unboundedly. Unlike prior violations based on biased guesses, the violation exploits zero-error certificates. This yields a dichotomy: either IC is a valid physical principle excluding these correlations, or any nonsignalling theory realizing them lacks a mutual information satisfying consistency, data processing, and the chain rule.
AI.conclusion: The result sharpens the boundary of IC and forces a choice between rejecting almost-quantum correlations on principle or relinquishing the chain rule for mutual information. The authors argue the chain rule is the natural property to give up, and relate this to histories-based formulations and to locality defined relative to the state rather than a fixed spacetime.

title: An Unbounded Separation of Almost-Quantum and Commuting-Operator Correlations in Zero-Error Communication
comment: 35 pages, single column, 2 figures; comments are welcome
summary: Almost-quantum correlations form the $\mathtt{1+AB}$ level of the Navascués--Pironio--Acín hierarchy. They strictly contain the quantum set, are characterized by a single semidefinite program, arise in Sorkin's quantum measure theory, and satisfy several principles proposed to single out quantum theory. We show that they are nevertheless unboundedly stronger than quantum correlations in a zero-error communication task. Alice and Bob receive labels $s,t\in[N]$, $N\ge3$; after one bit from Alice, Bob must decide whether $s=t$, never erring but allowed to abstain. For every model of quantum correlations, from finite-dimensional tensor products to commuting operators, the optimal worst-case probability of a conclusive answer is exactly $1/N$, the value attained with shared randomness, so the bound does not depend on the resolution of Tsirelson's problem. An explicit family of almost-quantum correlations attains $1/19$ for every $N$. For certificates of equality from binary-outcome boxes, we solve the underlying semidefinite programs in closed form. The almost-quantum optimum equals $N^2/(17N^2-80N+64)$ for $N\ge8$ and tends to $1/17$. The first level of the hierarchy, which coincides with the set singled out by macroscopic locality, attains $N/[8(N-2)]$, which tends to $1/8$; its optimal boxes lie outside the almost-quantum set for every $N\ge5$. For longer messages, entanglement saves at most one bit over shared randomness, whereas almost-quantum correlations reduce the one-way zero-error cost of deciding equality of $n$-bit strings from $n$ bits to at most $13$. The quantum bound also yields a linear witness of post-quantumness on a face of the nonsignalling polytope.

AI.tldr: Almost-quantum correlations, though physically well-motivated and strictly containing the quantum set, are unboundedly more powerful than any quantum correlation for zero-error equality certification: they compress the one-way zero-error cost of deciding equality of n-bit strings to at most 13 bits, while quantum correlations (under any resolution of Tsirelson's problem) perform no better than shared randomness.
AI.motivation: Almost-quantum correlations sit in the 1+AB level of the NPA hierarchy, strictly contain quantum correlations, satisfy several principles purported to single out quantum theory, and arise in Sorkin's quantum measure theory. The paper asks how powerful these ostensibly near-quantum correlations really are in a concrete zero-error communication task, thereby probing whether the proposed principles genuinely isolate quantum theory.
AI.method: A "certificate of equality" task is used: Alice and Bob receive labels s,t∈[N] (N≥3); after one bit from Alice, Bob must decide whether s=t, never erring but allowed to abstain. The optimal worst-case conclusive-answer probability is computed for (i) all quantum correlation models (finite-dimensional tensor products through commuting operators), (ii) an explicit family of almost-quantum correlations, and (iii) the first NPA level (macroscopic locality). For binary-outcome boxes the underlying semidefinite programs are solved in closed form; the analysis is extended to longer messages and n-bit strings.
AI.result: For every quantum model—finite-dimensional tensor products to commuting operators—the optimal worst-case conclusive probability is exactly 1/N, matching shared randomness, independent of the resolution of Tsirelson's problem. An explicit almost-quantum family attains 1/19 for every N. For binary-outcome equality certificates, the almost-quantum optimum is N²/(17N²−80N+64) for N≥8, tending to 1/17, while the first level (macroscopic locality) attains N/[8(N−2)], tending to 1/8; its optimal boxes fall outside the almost-quantum set for all N≥5. For longer messages, entanglement saves at most one bit over shared randomness, whereas almost-quantum correlations reduce the one-way zero-error cost of deciding equality of n-bit strings from n bits to at most 13.
AI.conclusion: Almost-quantum correlations are unboundedly stronger than quantum correlations in zero-error communication, sharply separating them despite their near-quantum pedigree. The quantum bound also yields a linear witness of post-quantumness on a face of the nonsignalling polytope. These results show that principles satisfied by almost-quantum correlations cannot single out quantum theory, and expose strict separations between the first NPA level, the almost-quantum set, and the quantum set.

title: eCAS: An Orbital Embedding Method for Quantum Computing
summary: Future fault-tolerant quantum computers will allow us to calculate electronic structures of atomistic systems. However, these systems will be intrinsically limited in size, requiring embedding theories for many systems because of the unfavorable scaling of the number of terms describing the electron-electron interaction in the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian. Quantum embedding theories address this challenge by partitioning a quantum system into a region of interest, the impurity, and its (larger) complement, the environment. However, currently available quantum embedding methods place restrictive demands on near-future quantum computers, such as the need to measure reduced density matrices or the need for repeated evaluations. Here, we introduce the new orbital embedding method eCAS that steers clear of these pitfalls by constructing a multi-CAS problem, the active spaces of which are localized and can be solved independently of each other with any quantum algorithm. This also allows for the development of comparatively simple gradient expressions. eCAS leverages the Schmidt decomposition to construct initial impurity and bath orbitals and augments them with localized environment orbitals, based on a mutual correlation criterion. The mutual correlation criterion makes eCAS systematically improvable without the need for any iteratively determined quantities.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces eCAS, an orbital embedding method that constructs a multi-CAS problem with localized, independently solvable active spaces, avoiding repeated evaluations or reduced-density-matrix measurements, enabled by a Schmidt-decomposition initialization and a mutual-correlation criterion.
AI.motivation: Near-term fault-tolerant quantum computers can compute electronic structures but are size-limited by the unfavorable scaling of the second-quantized Hamiltonian's electron-electron interaction terms. Quantum embedding addresses this by partitioning the system into an impurity and environment, yet existing embedding methods impose restrictive hardware demands such as measuring reduced density matrices or repeated evaluations.
AI.method: eCAS constructs a multi-CAS problem whose active spaces are localized and independently solvable with any quantum algorithm. It uses the Schmidt decomposition to build initial impurity and bath orbitals, then augments them with localized environment orbitals guided by a mutual correlation criterion. This design also yields comparatively simple gradient expressions and requires no iteratively determined quantities.
AI.result: The method avoids the pitfalls of reduced-density-matrix measurement and repeated evaluations required by prior quantum embedding approaches, while remaining systematically improvable via the mutual correlation criterion.
AI.conclusion: eCAS offers a hardware-friendly orbital embedding scheme enabling localized, parallelizable quantum active-space treatments with simple gradients and systematic improvability.

title: High-efficiency photonic GHZ measurements with linear optics
summary: Probabilistic and destructive Bell-measurements, also known as fusions, constitute a fundamental primitive for photonic quantum technologies. These operations rely only on pairwise photonic interference, whereas the computational power of photonic quantum systems originates from many-body interference. Here, we introduce a family of high-efficiency linear-optical GHZ measurements based on four-mode interferometers and show that incorporating many-body interference into this ubiquitous primitive leads to more efficient entangling operations. For the four-photon case, the success probability is $9/32$, and adaptive variants ensure that unsuccessful events project onto useful stabilizer states. We further show that the approach naturally generalizes to larger GHZ measurements, yielding an exponentially higher success probability than previous linear-optical schemes. Finally, we demonstrate practical advantages for graph-state resource generation, entanglement distribution between remote spin-photon interfaces, and fusion-based quantum computing. Our results establish high-efficiency many-body measurements as a new primitive for scalable photonic quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a family of high-efficiency linear-optical GHZ measurements built on four-mode interferometers, showing that embedding many-body interference into the fusion primitive yields more efficient entangling operations, higher success probabilities, and practical advantages for photonic quantum information processing.
AI.motivation: Standard photonic Bell measurements (fusions) rely only on pairwise photonic interference, yet the computational power of photonic systems stems from many-body interference. The authors aim to exploit this unexploited resource to make the ubiquitous fusion primitive more efficient.
AI.method: They design a family of high-efficiency linear-optical GHZ measurements based on four-mode interferometers, generalizing beyond pairwise interference. For the four-photon case they compute the success probability (9/32) and develop adaptive variants that project unsuccessful events onto useful stabilizer states. The construction is extended to larger GHZ measurements.
AI.result: The four-photon GHZ measurement achieves a success probability of 9/32, with adaptive variants recovering useful stabilizer states from failed events. The scheme generalizes to larger GHZ measurements with exponentially higher success probability than previous linear-optical schemes, and demonstrates practical advantages for graph-state resource generation, entanglement distribution between remote spin-photon interfaces, and fusion-based quantum computing.
AI.conclusion: High-efficiency many-body measurements are established as a new primitive for scalable photonic quantum information processing, offering a superior alternative to pairwise-interference-based fusions.

title: FaultScope: A software package for fast error attribution in quantum error correction
summary: We introduce FaultScope, a classical simulator for quantum error correction circuits, implemented in Rust with a Python interface. FaultScope estimates logical error rates and their derivatives with respect to component error rates from the same sampled and decoded shots, without modifying or differentiating through the decoder. These derivatives enable error attribution to individual noisy components, helping identify noise hotspots for targeted noise reduction. FaultScope supports forward simulation of error propagation through circuits and direct sampling of detector and logical observable outcomes from detector error models. In our noiseless and noisy benchmarks, FaultScope has the lowest runtime among the tested simulators at every size. Computing all derivatives adds only 0.33--0.97\% to the runtime of logical error rate estimation across five repetition code sizes with 7--2047 error locations. FaultScope can be used to benchmark large-scale quantum error correction schemes and guide targeted noise reduction efficiently, thereby facilitating the design and optimization of fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

AI.tldr: FaultScope is a Rust-based (Python-interfaced) classical simulator for quantum error correction circuits that estimates logical error rates and their derivatives w.r.t. component error rates from the same sampled shots, enabling error attribution and noise-hotspot identification, with the lowest runtime among tested simulators.
AI.motivation: Estimating logical error rates is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing design, but efficiently attributing logical errors to individual noisy components (to guide targeted noise reduction) is challenging, as it typically requires modifying or differentiating through the decoder. The authors aim to provide these derivatives essentially for free alongside standard logical error rate estimation.
AI.method: FaultScope simulates QEC circuits in Rust with a Python interface. It computes logical error rates and their derivatives w.r.t. component error rates from the same sampled and decoded shots, without modifying or differentiating through the decoder. It supports forward simulation of error propagation through circuits and direct sampling of detector and logical observable outcomes from detector error models.
AI.result: In noiseless and noisy benchmarks, FaultScope achieves the lowest runtime among tested simulators at every problem size. Computing all derivatives adds only 0.33–0.97% to the runtime of logical error rate estimation across five repetition-code sizes with 7–2047 error locations.
AI.conclusion: FaultScope enables efficient benchmarking of large-scale quantum error correction schemes and guided targeted noise reduction, facilitating the design and optimization of fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

title: Symmetries and model reduction in a $\cos 2\varphi$ transmon qubit
summary: Engineered symmetries in superconducting circuits can protect quantum information; much like selection rules in atomic physics, they forbid transitions between the qubit states. Protected circuits, however, combine several loops and islands and host multiple nonlinearly coupled modes, calling for reduced low-energy models that inherit the circuit symmetries and make the protection manifest. We develop such a reduction for the $\cos 2\varphi$ transmon qubit, recently realized experimentally with a two-Cooper-pair interferometer, whose circuit hosts three coupled modes. Exploiting the separation of energy scales between the heavy transmon mode and the light internal modes of the interferometer, we derive an effective single-band Born-Oppenheimer model, including its geometric correction, and extend it to several bands. We identify the symmetries of the full and reduced Hamiltonians and derive exact selection rules. Finally, we identify a parameter regime beyond the single-band description that suppresses flux-noise dephasing without degrading charge-noise protection.

AI.tldr: The authors derive a symmetry-preserving, effective Born-Oppenheimer reduction for the three-mode cos2φ transmon circuit, obtain exact selection rules from circuit symmetries, and identify a multiband regime that suppresses flux-noise dephasing while retaining charge-noise protection.
AI.motivation: Engineered symmetries in superconducting circuits can protect quantum information by forbidding transitions between qubit states, analogous to atomic selection rules. However, protected circuits combine multiple loops and islands and host several nonlinearly coupled modes, so simple low-energy models are inadequate; one needs reduced models that inherit the full circuit symmetries and make the protection explicit.
AI.method: Focusing on the cos2φ transmon qubit realized with a two-Cooper-pair interferometer and hosting three coupled modes, the authors exploit the separation of energy scales between the heavy transmon mode and the light internal interferometer modes. They derive an effective single-band Born-Oppenheimer model including its geometric (Berry-type) correction, extend it to multiple bands, identify the symmetries of the full and reduced Hamiltonians, and derive exact selection rules from them.
AI.result: The reduction yields a single-band Born-Oppenheimer Hamiltonian with geometric correction, generalized to several bands, together with identified symmetries of both full and reduced models and exact selection rules. A parameter regime beyond the single-band description is found in which flux-noise dephasing is suppressed without degrading charge-noise protection.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry-consistent effective models provide a systematic framework for protected superconducting qubits with multiple coupled modes, and multiband effects offer an additional knob to suppress flux-noise dephasing while preserving charge-noise protection.

title: Quantum Bernstein--Kolmogorov--Arnold approximation
summary:
This paper addresses the expressivity and representation gap in Quantum Neural Networks by establishing a quantum analogue of the classical Kolmogorov--Arnold representation theorem.
  We propose a constructive approximation framework over fixed input coherent states, where the dependence of the function argument is embedded entirely in coordinate qubits, while the target function dictates a single outer unitary evolution.
  By applying a Sprecher-type representation to the rotation angle of the state, we demonstrate that the multidimensional operator factorises into \(2d+1\) commuting universal inner observables.
  We prove that the resulting measurement probability precisely reproduces the multidimensional Bernstein polynomial of the target function.
  For any continuous multivariate function, the joint quantum state converges uniformly to the target output register, linking classical superposition theory with probabilistic and coherent quantum circuits.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a quantum analogue of the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem, showing that any continuous multivariate function can be uniformly approximated by a fixed-input-coherent-state quantum circuit whose multidimensional operator factorises into 2d+1 commuting universal inner observables, with measurement probabilities reproducing multidimensional Bernstein polynomials.
AI.motivation: Quantum Neural Networks suffer from an expressivity and representation gap; the authors seek a principled representational foundation by importing the classical Kolmogorov–Arnold superposition theory into the quantum setting.
AI.method: A constructive approximation framework is built over fixed input coherent states, embedding the function argument's dependence entirely in coordinate qubits while the target function determines a single outer unitary. A Sprecher-type representation is applied to the rotation angle of the state, factorising the multidimensional operator into 2d+1 commuting universal inner observables; the resulting measurement probability is proven to exactly reproduce the multidimensional Bernstein polynomial of the target function.
AI.result: The multidimensional operator is shown to decompose into 2d+1 commuting universal inner observables, and the measurement probability is proven to precisely match the multidimensional Bernstein polynomial of the target function; for any continuous multivariate function the joint quantum state converges uniformly to the target output register.
AI.conclusion: The work bridges classical superposition theory with probabilistic and coherent quantum circuits, offering a constructive route to universal function representation and closing part of the expressivity gap in Quantum Neural Networks.

title: Windowed Catodyne Measurements: Continuum Approximation versus Exact Discrete Photon-Number Treatment
summary: We analyze a family of measurements obtained by retaining only a finite window of the photon-sum variable in catodyne detection, where a Schrödinger cat state serves as the local oscillator. In the continuum approximation, the window half-width appears to act as a continuous knob for coherence. However, a treatment on the discrete photon-number lattice shows that, in the strong-LO regime, the coherence conditioned on the difference outcome is not suppressed by the window. The exact parity-sensitive success probability is a staircase function of and , whose plateau structure and magnitude the continuum formulas fail to capture, especially for small and narrow windows. For remote preparation of cat states, an exact calculation with a finitely squeezed resource shows that the remote state keeps a purity close to one when x is resolved, and loses purity mainly when x is not recorded. Our results clarify where the continuum approximation of catodyne detection can be trusted and where the discrete photon-number structure must be used.

AI.tldr: Catodyne detection with a photon-sum window is analyzed exactly on the discrete photon-number lattice. In the strong-LO regime the window does not suppress coherence, and the success probability is a staircase in the window bounds that continuum formulas miss.
AI.motivation: Catodyne detection (cat-state local oscillator) has been treated in a continuum approximation where a finite window on the photon-sum variable acts as a continuous coherence knob; the authors want to test where this picture holds and where the discrete photon-number structure dominates.
AI.method: Exact treatment of the measurement family that retains only a finite window of the photon-sum variable, computed on the discrete photon-number lattice rather than in the continuum limit, including an exact parity-sensitive success probability and a remote-preparation calculation with a finitely squeezed resource.
AI.result: In the strong-LO regime the coherence conditioned on the difference outcome is not suppressed by the window. The exact parity-sensitive success probability is a staircase function of the window parameters, with plateau structure and magnitude not captured by continuum formulas, especially for small and narrow windows. For remote cat-state preparation the remote state keeps purity close to one when the conjugate variable is resolved, and loses purity mainly when it is not recorded.
AI.conclusion: The continuum approximation of catodyne detection is reliable only in a restricted regime; outside it the discrete photon-number lattice must be used. The results delineate the trust region of the continuum description and identify measurement-record completeness (resolving the unrecorded variable) as the key to remote-state purity.

title: Quantum machine learning geospatial time-series by seasonal encoding
summary: Quantum data reuploading models can increase the expressive capacity of variational quantum models, but do not necessarily improve predictive performance. In the present work, we investigate this behavior for seasonal time series forecasting and show that data encoding determines how well temporal structures are represented as circuit depth increases. We develop a fidelity-based quantum geometric description in which repeated encodings contribute to an effective input generator, so that reuploading depth changes the quantum geometry through which approximately recurrent inputs are distinguished. We construct fixed and adaptive seasonal encodings that represent observation magnitude and seasonal phase in distinct Bloch-sphere coordinates. We evaluate these encodings for monthly precipitation derived from ERA5-Land, a global reanalysis dataset, from a representative semi-arid, drought-prone tropical region in East Africa, using a 14-month lag window and reuploading depths $L$= 1-6. We find that in ideal simulations, standard value-based encodings degrade markedly with depth, whereas adaptive seasonal encodings preserve temporal correlation, spectral structure, and forecasting accuracy. Noisy simulations show that this encoding hierarchy persists at shallow and intermediate depths, while larger depths are limited by circuit noise and optimization difficulty. The seasonal quantum models remain competitive with established classical forecasting methods (ARIMA, random forests, and LSTMs). These results identify structure-aware quantum data encoding as a general strategy for building deeper quantum reuploading models.

AI.tldr: Data-reuploading depth does not guarantee better forecasting; encoding choice governs how temporal structure is represented as depth grows, and structure-aware seasonal encodings preserve accuracy where standard value encodings degrade.
AI.motivation: Repeated data reuploading increases variational quantum model expressivity but does not reliably improve predictive performance. The paper investigates this gap for seasonal time series and asks how encoding determines whether temporal structure is preserved as circuit depth increases.
AI.method: A fidelity-based quantum geometric description is developed in which repeated encodings act as an effective input generator, so reuploading depth reshapes the geometry that distinguishes approximately recurrent inputs. Fixed and adaptive seasonal encodings map observation magnitude and seasonal phase onto distinct Bloch-sphere coordinates. Evaluation uses monthly precipitation from ERA5-Land for a semi-arid, drought-prone tropical East African region, with a 14-month lag window and reuploading depths L = 1–6, under both ideal and noisy simulation, benchmarked against ARIMA, random forests, and LSTMs.
AI.result: In ideal simulations, standard value-based encodings degrade markedly with depth, whereas adaptive seasonal encodings preserve temporal correlation, spectral structure, and forecasting accuracy. Noisy simulations retain this encoding hierarchy at shallow and intermediate depths, while larger depths are constrained by circuit noise and optimization difficulty. The seasonal quantum models remain competitive with classical baselines.
AI.conclusion: Structure-aware quantum data encoding is a general strategy for building deeper quantum reuploading models, since encoding rather than depth alone determines the representation of temporal structure.

title: Simulating two-Dimensional decaying vortex structure with the Carleman-Lattice-Boltzmann method
summary:
We perform a numerical study of the free decay of two-dimensional nonlinear vortex structures using the second-order-truncated Carleman-Lattice Boltzmann method (CLB2). To this purpose, we simulate the nonlinear vortex system on a $128\times128$ grid at two initial Reynolds numbers, $Re\approx15$ and $Re\approx46$, by resorting to a highly-tuned multi-GPU implementation of the CLB2 code.
  At $Re \approx 15$, CLB2 shows significant accuracy all along the decay process, up to six diffusive times (corresponding to $950$ time steps), with structure-preserving errors below 10\% in amplitude, where by structure-preserving we imply that such errors can be almost entirely reabsorbed by a global time-dependent rescaling factor. At $Re \approx 46$, the evolution is carried out over $2850$ time steps, also corresponding to six diffusive times. In this scenario, however, the errors grow in time well above 10\% in amplitude with a still relatively modest but appreciable effect on the spatial structure of the flow.
  These results indicate that CLB2 is capable of preserving the nonlinear evolution of coherent structures over sufficiently long time spans to reach an effective zero steady-state. However CLB2 shows a constant sub-dissipative trend (more energy than the corresponding Lattice Boltzmann configurations) with a deteriorating accuracy at increasing time and Reynolds number.
  The present results shed hope that further developments, such as suitable closures instead of truncation and/or various forms of regularization, may lead to a significant improvement of the CLB2 accuracy, prior or even without escalating to expensive higher-order truncations.

AI.tldr: Numerical study of free decay of 2D nonlinear vortex structures using second-order truncated Carleman-Lattice Boltzmann (CLB2) on a 128×128 grid at Re≈15 and Re≈46, showing structure-preserving accuracy over six diffusive times at low Re but growing errors and a sub-dissipative trend at higher Re.
AI.motivation: To assess whether the CLB2 method can faithfully preserve the nonlinear long-time evolution of coherent vortex structures, and to quantify how accuracy degrades with increasing time and Reynolds number relative to standard Lattice Boltzmann configurations.
AI.method: Simulated free decay of 2D nonlinear vortex structures with the second-order-truncated Carleman-Lattice Boltzmann method (CLB2) on a 128×128 grid at Re≈15 (950 steps) and Re≈46 (2850 steps), both spanning six diffusive times, using a highly-tuned multi-GPU CLB2 implementation. Errors were decomposed into amplitude and spatial-structure components, with a global time-dependent rescaling factor used to measure structure-preserving error.
AI.result: At Re≈15, CLB2 achieves structure-preserving amplitude errors below 10% throughout the decay to six diffusive times. At Re≈46, errors grow well above 10% in amplitude with a modest but appreciable distortion of the spatial flow structure. CLB2 exhibits a constant sub-dissipative trend (retaining more energy than corresponding Lattice Boltzmann configurations), with accuracy deteriorating at longer times and higher Reynolds numbers.
AI.conclusion: CLB2 can preserve the nonlinear evolution of coherent structures over sufficiently long spans to reach an effective zero steady-state, but its sub-dissipative bias and degrading accuracy at higher Re/time limit its fidelity. The authors suggest that suitable closures replacing truncation and/or regularization schemes could substantially improve CLB2 accuracy without escalating to expensive higher-order truncations.

title: Solving the MAX-$k$-CUT problem for hypergraphs with quantum computing
summary: We investigate the MAX-$k$-CUT problem on hypergraphs by considering their representation as spin systems with Ising interactions. The corresponding cost Hamiltonian for MAX-$k$-CUT problem on hypergraphs is reduced to an Ising Hamiltonian with pairwise interactions. This reduction simplifies the solution of the MAX-$k$-CUT problem using quantum computing. As illustrative examples, a 3-uniform tight-star hypergraph and a sunflower hypergraph are considered. The corresponding Hamiltonians are constructed, and quantum protocols for the MAX-$k$-CUT problems are presented. The MAX-3-CUT and MAX-4-CUT instances are investigated for these hypergraphs by varying the number of Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) layers from (p=2) to (p=15) with quantum computing on IBM's Qiskit AerSimulator.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates MAX-k-CUT on hypergraphs as a pairwise-interaction Ising cost Hamiltonian, enabling simpler quantum solving, and demonstrates QAOA protocols on specific hypergraph families.
AI.motivation: MAX-k-CUT on hypergraphs involves high-order (multi-body) interactions that complicate quantum implementation. Reducing the problem to a representation with only pairwise Ising interactions can simplify and make feasible its solution on quantum hardware.
AI.method: Hypergraphs are modeled as spin systems with Ising interactions. The MAX-k-CUT cost Hamiltonian is reduced to an Ising Hamiltonian with pairwise interactions. Two illustrative hypergraph families—a 3-uniform tight-star hypergraph and a sunflower hypergraph—are analyzed: their Hamiltonians are constructed and quantum protocols (QAOA) are presented. MAX-3-CUT and MAX-4-CUT instances are evaluated with QAOA layer counts p=2 through p=15 on IBM's Qiskit AerSimulator.
AI.result: The reduction to a pairwise Ising Hamiltonian was achieved, and corresponding Hamiltonians and quantum protocols were constructed for the tight-star and sunflower hypergraphs. QAOA simulations for MAX-3-CUT and MAX-4-CUT were run with p ranging from 2 to 15, showing the effect of layer depth on performance.
AI.conclusion: Representing MAX-k-CUT on hypergraphs as a pairwise Ising Hamiltonian simplifies its quantum solution, and QAOA is a viable approach for these instances, with deeper circuits explored for improved solutions.

title: Exponential quantum-classical query separations for cyclic Forrelation
summary:
We study the randomized classical query complexity of cyclic Forrelation, a cyclic analogue of $k$-Forrelation [AA15, STOC'15; BS21, STOC'21]. Given $k$ Boolean functions $f_1,\ldots,f_k:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\{-1,1\}$, the goal is to estimate $T_k=N^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(D_{f_1}H^{\otimes n}\cdots D_{f_k}H^{\otimes n}),$ where $D_{f_i}=\operatorname{diag}(f_i(x):x\in\mathbb{F}_2^n)$, $H$ is the Hadamard gate, and $N=2^n$. This normalized-trace problem can be solved with $k$ quantum queries in the DQC1 model. Its classical query complexity was left open in [JLS+26, FOCS'26], which conjectured a lower bound of $\widetildeΩ(N^{1-2/k})$.
  We establish a nearly complete characterization of the nonadaptive classical query complexity of cyclic Forrelation. For even $k\ge 4$, we prove a tight bound of $Θ_k(N^{1-2/k})$ for constant additive error. For odd $k\ge 5$, we obtain a lower bound of $Ω_k(N^{1-2/(k-1)})$ and an upper bound of $O_k(N^{1-2/k})$. Surprisingly, $k=3$ admits a polylogarithmic-query nonadaptive classical algorithm, disproving the conjecture in this case. These results suggest an unexpected parity-dependent structure: the nonadaptive complexity may be governed by the independence number of the $k$-cycle, leading to the exponent $1-1/\lfloor k/2\rfloor$, rather than the previously conjectured $1-2/k$, which was motivated by a Fourier-growth heuristic. Finally, allowing adaptivity, we prove a lower bound of $Ω(N^{1/4})$ for every $k\ge4$.
  Although formally close to $k$-Forrelation, the cyclic structure leads to rather different classical behavior and requires different techniques. Our lower bounds are based on hidden-shift collision constructions, and our upper bounds follow from randomized sampling together with cycle-specific conditional-moment estimates. Our results provide a systematic understanding of its query advantages over classical computation.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes the nonadaptive classical query complexity of cyclic Forrelation, proving tight bounds for even k, separating odd k, and showing k=3 admits a polylogarithmic classical algorithm (refuting the prior conjecture).
AI.motivation: Cyclic Forrelation is solvable with k quantum queries in the DQC1 model, but its classical query complexity was left open; a prior conjecture (JLS+26) posited a lower bound of Õ(N^{1-2/k}) motivated by a Fourier-growth heuristic.
AI.method: Lower bounds via hidden-shift collision constructions; upper bounds via randomized sampling combined with cycle-specific conditional-moment estimates.
AI.result: Even k≥4: tight Θ_k(N^{1-2/k}). Odd k≥5: lower bound Ω_k(N^{1-2/(k-1)}), upper bound O_k(N^{1-2/k}). k=3: polylogarithmic nonadaptive classical algorithm. Adaptive setting: Ω(N^{1/4}) for all k≥4.
AI.conclusion: Nonadaptive complexity appears governed by the independence number of the k-cycle, giving exponent 1-1/⌊k/2⌋ rather than the conjectured 1-2/k—an unexpected parity-dependent structure; adaptivity yields only a weaker Ω(N^{1/4}) bound.

title: Extending Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization to Systems of Linear Equations
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Code: Python package sqd_linsolve (MIT License) with two notebooks in the ancillary files: reproduce_paper.ipynb reproduces the numerical results of the paper; sqd_linear_systems_selfcontained.ipynb gives a self-contained, step-by-step implementation with explanations and a worked example
summary: Solving systems of linear equations, $Ax=b$, is a ubiquitous task in computational science. The Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd algorithm requires phase estimation, controlled rotations, and post-selection, impractical on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware. We extend sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), developed for quantum chemistry, to linear systems. Following the sample-based Krylov variant, the Hermitian matrix $A$ is decomposed in the Pauli basis, the Trotterized time evolution of $|b\rangle$ is sampled at several times to select computational-basis configurations, and the system is solved classically by a Galerkin projection onto the selected subspace.
