We prove that the subspace solution is exact when the sampled configurations contain the Krylov support of $b$ and optimal in the energy norm for symmetric positive-definite matrices, so that noise-induced configurations cannot degrade it as long as they do not displace the ideal ones. On IBM Quantum hardware, the sampled distribution of a $4\times4$ example deviates from the exact one by eleven times the shot-noise level, yet the solution is recovered exactly. For a localized problem of dimension $N=1024$, SQD selects 33 configurations, reaches a relative error of $10^{-5}$, and its truncated subspaces coincide with the optimal choice; readout errors enlarge the subspace without degrading the accuracy. The tests also show the limitations: the selected subspace coincides with that of inexpensive classical selection, banded matrices require exponentially many Pauli terms in the binary encoding, and Trotter errors populate spurious configurations unless the circuits are deep. An MIT-licensed Python package and notebooks that reproduce the numerical results are provided.

AI.tldr: The authors extend sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) from quantum chemistry to solving linear systems $Ax=b$, decomposing $A$ in the Pauli basis, sampling Trotterized time evolution to select a subspace, and solving via classical Galerkin projection, with proofs of exactness/optimality and hardware validation recovering exact solutions despite noisy sampling.
AI.motivation: The Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd algorithm for linear systems requires phase estimation, controlled rotations, and post-selection, making it impractical on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. A NISQ-friendly alternative is needed that avoids these expensive primitives.
AI.method: SQD is extended to linear systems following the sample-based Krylov variant: the Hermitian matrix $A$ is decomposed in the Pauli basis; the Trotterized time evolution of $|b\rangle$ is sampled at several times to select computational-basis configurations; and the system is solved classically by Galerkin projection onto the selected subspace.
AI.result: They prove the subspace solution is exact when sampled configurations contain the Krylov support of $b$, and optimal in the energy norm for symmetric positive-definite matrices, so noise-induced configurations cannot degrade it unless they displace the ideal ones. On IBM Quantum hardware, a $4\times4$ example's sampled distribution deviates by eleven times the shot-noise level yet the solution is recovered exactly. For $N=1024$, SQD selects 33 configurations, reaching relative error $10^{-5}$, with truncated subspaces coinciding with the optimal choice; readout errors enlarge the subspace without degrading accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The approach is validated but has limitations: the selected subspace coincides with inexpensive classical selection, banded matrices require exponentially many Pauli terms in binary encoding, and Trotter errors populate spurious configurations unless circuits are deep. An MIT-licensed Python package and reproducibility notebooks are provided.

title: A Highly Nondegenerate Photon-Pair Source for Detector-Matched Quantum Key Distribution
summary: In a commercial entanglement-distribution system over telecom fibre, the single-photon detectors are the largest part of the hardware cost. In entanglement-based quantum key distribution (QKD), both photons of each pair must be detected. With two telecom photons, each arm needs either an InGaAs single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) of low efficiency or a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SNSPD) with its own cryostat. We study a highly nondegenerate photon-pair source that needs a telecom detector on one arm only. Two periodically poled KTiOPO$_4$ (ppKTP) crystals pumped at 405~nm emit pairs at 548 and 1550~nm. A Si-SPAD with 82\% efficiency detects the 548~nm photon at the source node, and only the 1550~nm photon travels through fibre. A first, unoptimised module in a polarisation-correlated configuration generates about $1.5\times10^6$ pairs/s per mW of pump power. It collects 13\% of the pairs on the 548~nm arm and 23\% on the 1550~nm arm. In an asymptotic BBM92 model, we compare its links with generic $2\times1550$~nm links that use a bright published source at the same pump power. At 50~km, our link with one SNSPD costs about 25\% more per secret bit than the generic link with one SNSPD. With optimistic target values of 52\% collection and twice the brightness, it costs about 40\% as much as the generic link with two SNSPDs. Our link without a cryostat then costs about 70\% less than the generic link with one SNSPD. If every link runs at its own best pump power, the two-SNSPD link is again the cheapest. The source can also serve clock synchronisation and detector calibration, which need only time-correlated pairs. All key rates assume the entangled configuration of the source, which is under development.

AI.tldr: A highly nondegenerate photon-pair source (548 nm + 1550 nm) allows detection at the source node with a high-efficiency Si-SPAD and transmission of only the telecom photon, cutting detector cost; an unoptimised module reaches ~1.5×10^6 pairs/s/mW and, with optimistic targets, a one-SNSPD link costs ~40% of a two-SNSPD generic link.
AI.motivation: Single-photon detectors dominate hardware cost in commercial entanglement-distribution systems over telecom fibre. Entanglement-based QKD requires detection of both photons, so a standard 2×1550 nm link needs either two low-efficiency InGaAs SPADs or two SNSPDs each with a cryostat, making it expensive.
AI.method: Two periodically poled KTiOPO4 (ppKTP) crystals pumped at 405 nm emit highly nondegenerate photon pairs at 548 and 1550 nm. An 82%-efficiency Si-SPAD detects the 548 nm photon at the source node, so only the 1550 nm photon traverses fibre. A first unoptimised module is built in a polarisation-correlated configuration. An asymptotic BBM92 model compares its links against generic 2×1550 nm links using a bright published source at equal pump power, with variants differing in number of SNSPDs, collection efficiency, brightness, and per-link optimal pump power.
AI.result: The unoptimised module generates ~1.5×10^6 pairs/s per mW pump, collecting 13% of pairs on the 548 nm arm and 23% on the 1550 nm arm. At 50 km, the link with one SNSPD costs ~25% more per secret bit than the generic link with one SNSPD. With optimistic targets (52% collection, 2× brightness), it costs ~40% of the generic link with two SNSPDs, and without a cryostat ~70% less than the generic one-SNSPD link. If each link runs at its own best pump power, the two-SNSPD link is again cheapest.
AI.conclusion: Nondegenerate pair sources can shift detection to a cheap, high-efficiency Si-SPAD at the source node and materially reduce detector cost in telecom entanglement distribution, though the advantage is conditional on improved collection efficiency and brightness and on per-link pump-power optimisation. The source also supports clock synchronisation and detector calibration using time-correlated pairs. All key rates assume the entangled configuration, which is still under development.

title: Device-independent conference key agreement from two-body correlators with balanced Dicke states
summary: Device-independent conference key agreement (DI-CKA) enables $N > 2$ distant parties to establish a common secret key without detailed characterization of the source or measurement devices. Many existing protocols rely on full-body Bell correlators, whose measurement can be demanding for a large number of parties. Here, we show that two-body correlators alone suffice for DI-CKA using balanced Dicke states for every even $N \geq 4$. We construct two-body Bell inequalities and derive a tight analytical lower bound on the conditional von Neumann entropy by comparing their Bell operators with those of asymmetric Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt inequalities. In the ideal setting, certified key rates can approach $1-h[(N-2)/(4(N-1))]$, where $h$ is the binary entropy function. This rate remains bounded away from zero as $N \rightarrow \infty$, tending to $1-h(1/4) \approx 0.189$ bits per key-generation round. We show that the honest implementation of our protocol is invariant under collective phase noise. Moreover, a complementary full-body Bell construction certifies positive conference-key rates from correlations arbitrarily close to the local set.

AI.tldr: Two-body correlators alone suffice for device-independent conference key agreement (DI-CKA) using balanced Dicke states for every even N ≥ 4, with key rates that stay bounded away from zero as N grows.
AI.motivation: Existing DI-CKA protocols rely on full-body Bell correlators, which are demanding to measure for many parties. The authors aim to reduce the measurement complexity to two-body correlators while retaining device independence for N > 2 parties.
AI.method: The authors construct two-body Bell inequalities and derive a tight analytical lower bound on the conditional von Neumann entropy by comparing their Bell operators with those of asymmetric Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequalities, using balanced Dicke states.
AI.result: In the ideal setting, certified key rates approach 1 − h[(N−2)/(4(N−1))], which tends to 1 − h(1/4) ≈ 0.189 bits per round as N → ∞. The honest implementation is invariant under collective phase noise, and a complementary full-body Bell construction certifies positive rates from correlations arbitrarily close to the local set.
AI.conclusion: DI-CKA with only two-body correlators is feasible for all even N ≥ 4, yielding practical, noise-tolerant protocols with non-vanishing asymptotic key rates and reduced measurement demands.

title: Leveraging Quantum Measurement Randomness for Shot-Efficient Diffusion Models
summary: In quantum computing, the readout always carries finite-shot sampling noise. Suppressing this noise through repeated measurements raises the cost of a quantum neural network (QNN). Meanwhile, a stochastic diffusion sampler deliberately adds randomness at each reverse (generation) step. This paper turns the measurement noise from a liability into a resource. Specifically, we use the noise quantum measurement produces anyway to replace part of the noise the sampler would otherwise inject. We characterize the measurement error as multinomial sampling noise propagated through a trainable linear readout. To connect the circuit's Born probabilities to the denoising task, we further formulate the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex. Therefore, we can employ a compensation noise to match the mean and covariance of the shot-noise-free linear update under some minimum shot conditions. Solving this condition for the shot count gives a state-dependent adaptive budget. For the denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM), this budget increases as the sampler becomes more deterministic. On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the schedule achieves comparable generation quality with $303$ shots per sample against a high-shot reference of $1.6\times10^{6}$, about $5300\times$ fewer. Latent diffusion experiments on MNIST further validate the proposed mechanism for generation in a learned latent space.

AI.tldr: The paper repurposes finite-shot measurement noise in quantum neural networks as a substitute for part of the stochastic noise injected by diffusion samplers, deriving a state-dependent adaptive shot budget that achieves comparable generation quality with ~5300× fewer shots.
AI.motivation: Readout in quantum computing carries finite-shot sampling noise, and suppressing it via repeated measurements raises the cost of QNNs. Meanwhile, diffusion samplers deliberately add noise at each reverse step. The authors seek to turn the former liability into a resource by reusing unavoidable measurement noise to replace injected sampler noise.
AI.method: Measurement error is characterized as multinomial sampling noise propagated through a trainable linear readout. The diffusion process is formulated on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex to connect Born probabilities with the denoising task. A compensation noise is used to match the mean and covariance of the shot-noise-free linear update under minimum shot conditions, and solving this condition yields a state-dependent adaptive shot budget; for DDIM the budget grows as the sampler becomes more deterministic.
AI.result: On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the schedule achieves comparable generation quality with 303 shots per sample versus a high-shot reference of 1.6×10^6, roughly 5300× fewer. Latent diffusion experiments on MNIST further validate the mechanism for generation in a learned latent space.
AI.conclusion: Finite-shot measurement noise can be productively repurposed as the stochastic component of diffusion sampling, enabling a principled, state-adaptive shot allocation that drastically reduces quantum readout cost while preserving generation quality.

title: Scaling laws of entanglement entropy in fractal dimensions
summary: Entanglement entropy scaling links geometry to quantum correlations and diagnoses quantum criticality. Fractal lattices extend this link to noninteger dimensions, where boundary and bulk dimensions are independent. It remains open which dimension governs entropy scaling and how strongly gap closing can enhance it. Nonlocal occupied-state projectors and the lack of translation symmetry obstruct standard methods. We overcome these obstacles and classify free-fermion entropy scaling with bounds set by the hopping across the subsystem boundary: an upper bound from its rank and the spectral gap, and a lower bound from how much it lowers the ground-state energy. With only negative-energy states filled and this energy lowering proportional to the boundary, the entanglement entropy obeys the boundary law $S_X=Θ\left(L_X^{d_{\mathrm b}}\right)$ under a uniform gap and satisfies $L_X^{d_{\mathrm b}}\lesssim S_X\lesssim L_X^{d_{\mathrm b}}\ln L_X$ when the gap closes no faster than algebraically. Here $L_X$ is the subsystem linear size and $d_{\mathrm b}$ the boundary dimension. Half occupation of the chiral zero modes gives a mixed-state entropy $S_X^{\mathrm{mix}}$ with $\max\left\{S_X,z_X\ln2\right\}\leqslant S_X^{\mathrm{mix}}\leqslant S_X+z_X\ln2$, where $z_X$ is the local zero-mode weight; an extensive $z_X$ thus makes $S_X^{\mathrm{mix}}$ follow the bulk dimension.

AI.tldr: The authors classify free-fermion entanglement entropy scaling on fractal lattices, showing that entropy is governed by the boundary dimension d_b (not the bulk dimension) via bounds set by the hopping across the subsystem boundary, and that gap closing can at most add a logarithmic enhancement.
AI.motivation: Fractal lattices decouple boundary and bulk dimensions, so it is unclear which dimension controls entanglement entropy scaling and how strongly gap closing enhances it. Standard tools fail because occupied-state projectors are nonlocal and translation symmetry is absent.
AI.method: The authors derive an upper bound on entropy from the rank and spectral gap of the boundary-crossing hopping and a lower bound from the energy lowering the hopping induces; they apply these to half-filled chiral zero modes to obtain a mixed-state entropy relation involving the local zero-mode weight z_X.
AI.result: For negative-energy-filled states with energy lowering proportional to the boundary, S_X = Θ(L_X^{d_b}) under a uniform gap, and L_X^{d_b} ≲ S_X ≲ L_X^{d_b} ln L_X when the gap closes algebraically. For half-occupied chiral zero modes, max{S_X, z_X ln2} ≤ S_X^mix ≤ S_X + z_X ln2, so an extensive z_X makes S_X^mix follow the bulk dimension.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement entropy scaling on fractal lattices is set by the boundary dimension, with gap closing giving only logarithmic enhancement; mixed-state entropy switches to bulk-dimension scaling when zero modes are extensively occupied.

title: Chiral Torsional Double Wells: Tunneling and Polarizability
summary: Quantum tunneling between mirror-related wells of a torsional potential sets the timescale for coherent interconversion of chiral conformers. We ask whether slower tunneling also weakens the transition polarizability in hydrogen peroxide, hydrogen disulfide, and hydrogen diselenide. We use relaxed CCSD(T)//MP2 potentials and a kinetic model that removes overall molecular rotation to obtain the torsional states, then use static polarizabilities to calculate transition matrix elements between them. In the molecular frame used here, symmetry makes the matrix element of the even dipole component vanish between opposite-parity torsional states, while the odd polarizability component has a nonzero matrix element. The two quantities probe different parts of the torsional landscape: tunneling depends on penetration through the barriers, while the polarizability matrix element forms mainly within the wells. Consequently, tunneling slows sharply across the molecular series even as the matrix element grows. Higher torsional doublets and deuterium substitution further show that large changes in tunneling time can occur with little change in the transition polarizability matrix element. Calculated torsional energies for H$_2$O$_2$ and D$_2$O$_2$ agree with experimental values. Thus, slowing coherent interconversion need not weaken the intrinsic transition polarizability.

AI.tldr: Tunneling timescale and transition polarizability are decoupled: slowing coherent interconversion does not weaken the intrinsic transition polarizability across the H2O2, H2S2, H2Se2 series.
AI.motivation: Quantum tunneling between mirror-related wells sets the timescale of coherent chiral interconversion, and the authors test whether slower tunneling also weakens the transition polarizability linking opposite-parity torsional states.
AI.method: Relaxed CCSD(T)//MP2 torsional potentials with a kinetic model removing overall rotation give torsional states; static polarizabilities yield transition matrix elements. In the molecular frame, symmetry nulls the even dipole component between opposite-parity states while the odd polarizability component remains nonzero.
AI.result: Tunneling slows sharply across H2O2, H2S2, H2Se2 even as the polarizability matrix element grows, because tunneling depends on barrier penetration while the matrix element forms mainly within the wells. Higher torsional doublets and D substitution show large tunneling-time changes with little change in the transition polarizability. Calculated torsional energies for H2O2 and D2O2 agree with experiment.
AI.conclusion: Tunneling and the transition polarizability probe different regions of the torsional landscape and are largely decoupled; slowing coherent interconversion need not weaken the intrinsic transition polarizability.

title: Bounding Fidelity of Non-Stabilizer States from Local Pauli Measurements
summary: Nonstabilizerness, commonly referred to as magic, is essential for universal quantum computation. Yet, for pure $n$-qubit states this property is directly linked to the hardness of direct fidelity estimation. We propose a scheme to bound the fidelity on non-stabilizer states by choosing operators with low measurement overhead and using parallel local Pauli measurements to estimate compatible observables. We selectively measure operators that share a permutational symmetry without imposing any assumption on the physical system. This selection reduces the optimization to a linear program with only $O(n)$ variables for bounding fidelity. Our methods can be extended to bound nonlinear quantities like the purity via convex quadratic programs. For hypergraph states that can exhibit extensive nonstabilizerness, we demonstrate for up to $n=500$ qubits that our framework substantially reduces the measurement overhead under both local and global depolarizing noise. These results show that symmetry induced by measurement selection reduces both measurement and computational costs, enabling scalable characterization of magic resources in quantum computing and quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes symmetry-restricted measurement selection to bound fidelity (and purity) of non-stabilizer/hypergraph states with only O(n) optimization variables, reducing measurement and computational overhead for scalable magic characterization.
AI.motivation: Nonstabilizerness (magic) is necessary for universal quantum computation, but for pure n-qubit states it is directly tied to the hardness of direct fidelity estimation. Existing fidelity-estimation approaches incur prohibitive measurement overhead, motivating methods that bound fidelity on non-stabilizer states efficiently.
AI.method: Choose low-measurement-overhead operators and use parallel local Pauli measurements to estimate compatible observables. Select operators sharing a permutational symmetry (without assumptions on the physical system), which reduces the fidelity-bounding optimization to a linear program with only O(n) variables. Extend the approach to nonlinear quantities such as purity via convex quadratic programs.
AI.result: For hypergraph states exhibiting extensive nonstabilizerness, up to n=500 qubits are demonstrated to show substantial reduction in measurement overhead under both local and global depolarizing noise.
AI.conclusion: Measurement-selection-induced symmetry reduces both measurement and computational costs, enabling scalable characterization of magic resources in quantum computing and quantum networks.

title: Overcoming the Representational Limitations of Amplitude Encoding for Quantum Neural Networks
summary: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) offer a framework for learning functions from classical data, but their expressive power depends critically on how inputs are encoded into quantum states. Angle encoding can require resources that scale with the number of features, whereas amplitude encoding represents $d$ features using only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2 d)$ qubits. This compactness comes at a representational cost: normalization makes conventional amplitude encoding invariant to nonzero real rescaling of the input, up to an unobservable global phase. We show that this invariance induces an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the resulting hypothesis class. No downstream quantum circuit can distinguish inputs differing by nonzero real scaling. We develop a general condition under which deterministic preprocessing can remove this ambiguity and show that nonlinearity alone is insufficient. Based on this analysis, we introduce a fixed nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs under subsequent amplitude encoding, without adding trainable parameters and while retaining logarithmic qubit scaling. We evaluate the resulting QNN on three canonical classification benchmarks and a nonlinear synthetic dataset against conventional amplitude and angle encoding, as well as a classical neural network. Across these tasks, the proposed encoding consistently improves classification accuracy over both quantum encoding baselines by 21$-$44 %. Our results establish normalization-induced scale invariance as a concrete representational bottleneck of amplitude encoding and demonstrate that it can be removed while preserving a compact quantum representation, marking a step toward quantum models capable of capturing arbitrary relationships in classical data.

AI.tldr: Amplitude encoding's normalization makes QNNs invariant to nonzero real scaling of inputs, an architecture-independent restriction. The authors introduce a fixed nonlinear feature map that removes this ambiguity while keeping O(log d) qubit scaling and no extra trainable parameters, improving accuracy 21–44% over amplitude and angle encoding baselines.
AI.motivation: Angle encoding scales with the number of features, while amplitude encoding uses only O(log2 d) qubits but is invariant to nonzero real rescaling of inputs due to normalization. This scale invariance is a hidden representational bottleneck that no downstream quantum circuit can overcome.
AI.method: The paper proves the normalization-induced scale invariance is an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the hypothesis class, and derives a general condition for deterministic preprocessing to remove the ambiguity. It shows nonlinearity alone is insufficient, then proposes a fixed (non-trainable) nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs prior to amplitude encoding, preserving logarithmic qubit scaling.
AI.result: Evaluated on three canonical classification benchmarks plus a nonlinear synthetic dataset, against conventional amplitude encoding, angle encoding, and a classical neural network, the proposed encoding consistently improves accuracy over both quantum baselines by 21–44%.
AI.conclusion: Normalization-induced scale invariance is a concrete representational bottleneck of amplitude encoding, and it can be removed via a fixed nonlinear feature map while retaining a compact quantum representation, advancing QNNs toward capturing arbitrary relationships in classical data.

title: Toward Quantum Monte Carlo for Sovereign Debt Risk: A proof of concept
summary: We present a proof-of-concept pipeline that applies quantum amplitude estimation to the probability that a sovereign debt-to-GDP ratio exceeds a critical threshold at a given horizon. The pipeline combines a reduced two-factor Gaussian debt model linearized around its mean, quantum state preparation on a 32 x 32 grid, a weighted-adder circuit, an integer comparator, and Maximum Likelihood Amplitude Estimation (MLAE). On a noiseless statevector simulator with 500 shots per Grover power, the circuit estimate (a = 0.1152) agrees with the circuit's exact target amplitude (0.1153), and the observed estimation error is consistent with the amplitude-estimation scaling in the number of oracle calls. The model used here is deliberately simple: it admits a closed-form solution, so the contribution is a demonstration of the encoding and estimation workflow, not a practical advantage over classical methods. We discuss the conditions under which such a pipeline could become relevant and the obstacles that remain.

AI.tldr: A proof-of-concept quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) pipeline estimates the probability that a sovereign debt-to-GDP ratio breaches a threshold, achieving accuracy consistent with theoretical QAE scaling on a noiseless simulator, but offering no practical advantage over classical closed-form solutions.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to demonstrate a workflow for encoding and estimating a relevant financial risk quantity (threshold-breach probability of a debt-to-GDP ratio) using quantum amplitude estimation, exploring the feasibility of quantum methods for such probability computations.
AI.method: A reduced two-factor Gaussian debt model linearized around its mean, with a 32x32 grid quantum state preparation, a weighted-adder circuit, an integer comparator, and Maximum Likelihood Amplitude Estimation (MLAE) using 500 shots per Grover power on a noiseless statevector simulator.
AI.result: The circuit estimate (a = 0.1152) agrees with the circuit's exact target amplitude (0.1153), and the observed estimation error is consistent with the amplitude-estimation scaling in the number of oracle calls.
AI.conclusion: The deliberately simple model admits a closed-form solution, so the contribution is a demonstration of the encoding and estimation workflow rather than a practical advantage over classical methods. The authors discuss conditions for future relevance and remaining obstacles.

title: Engineered Learning Problems on Noisy Quantum Processors
summary: Despite quantum machine learning being an active topic of research, demonstrations of algorithms run on quantum hardware beating classical methods remain rare. In this work, we demonstrate a significant performance gap using a projected quantum kernel for $n=15,30$ and $45$ qubits over classical methods on an engineered classification problem, and show reproducibility of the results over different quantum processor units. We also demonstrate how error mitigation can widen this gap, both by improving hardware performance but also by increasing the classical difficulty, with different techniques contributing unequally to these phenomena. This work provides strong evidence that superior empirical performance of quantum hardware over all classical techniques is an achievable goal in quantum machine learning, albeit for an artificial problem. However, as with any application relying on observables, beating state-of-the-art simulation methods remains the primary challenge, as our matrix product state results here show.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates that a projected quantum kernel on 15–45 qubits significantly outperforms classical methods on an engineered classification task, reproducibly across quantum processing units, and that error mitigation widens the gap—while matrix product state simulations remain the main competitor.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning is heavily researched, yet empirical demonstrations of quantum hardware actually beating classical methods are rare. The authors aim to provide concrete evidence of a quantum advantage on quantum hardware for a classification task.
AI.method: Uses a projected quantum kernel to solve an engineered classification problem with n = 15, 30, and 45 qubits, running on multiple quantum processor units to test reproducibility. Applies error mitigation techniques and analyzes their unequal contributions to hardware performance improvement versus increased classical difficulty, and benchmarks against matrix product state (tensor-network) simulation.
AI.result: A significant performance gap is observed between the projected quantum kernel and classical methods, reproducible across different quantum processor units. Error mitigation widens this gap both by improving hardware performance and by increasing classical difficulty, with different techniques contributing unequally. However, matrix product state results show that beating state-of-the-art simulation methods remains the primary challenge.
AI.conclusion: The work provides strong evidence that superior empirical performance of quantum hardware over all classical techniques is achievable in quantum machine learning, albeit only for an artificial problem. For applications relying on observables, outperforming advanced classical simulation (e.g., matrix product states) remains the central obstacle.

title: Hybrid Quantum Algorithms for Trade Surveillance Analytics
summary: Anti-money laundering (AML) and trade surveillance remain largely manual: rule-based monitoring raises alerts of which, by estimate, over 95% are false positives, each reviewed by a human analyst. We benchmark four quantum and hybrid classifiers against classical baselines on a synthetic pump-and-dump detection task: a fidelity-based quantum k-nearest-neighbours classifier (QKNN) with clustering-based routing; a quantum support vector machine (QSVM) on a one-body projected quantum kernel; a 20-qubit quantum neural network (QNN) with a Pauli-ZZ feature map and RealAmplitudes ansatz; and a hybrid quantum neural network (HQNN) in which a small classical network generates every rotation angle of a five-qubit circuit. Baselines are logistic regression, XGBoost, one- and three-hidden-layer neural networks, and classical k-nearest neighbours. All models share one stratified split of 1000 accounts (800 train, 200 test, 20% suspicious) and two 20-feature representations (ANOVA and PCA); QKNN and QSVM are also tested under simulated noise, and the HQNN is run on the ibm_fez processor. The best model is classical XGBoost on ANOVA features, at a suspicious-class F1 of 61.4%. The HQNN is the strongest quantum-hybrid model, at 54.5-57.9% F1 on an ideal simulator and 55.4-59.8% on ibm_fez, ahead of six of eight classical configurations; at a 15% false-positive rate, half its alerts are genuinely suspicious. Versus the QNN (42.0% F1), it raises under half the false alarms at similar recall with a quarter of the qubits. The QKNN reaches 43.5% F1 (44.4% under noise), above classical KNN (35.6%); the QSVM does not exceed 41%. We observe no quantum advantage, but a five-qubit hybrid on today's noisy hardware already matches well-tuned classical models, with room to grow via richer circuits and larger devices. We contribute a like-for-like comparison with classical models on shared data, splits and features.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks four quantum/hybrid classifiers against classical baselines on synthetic pump-and-dump detection; no quantum advantage found, but a 5-qubit HQNN matches tuned classical models on real hardware (54.5–59.8% F1).
AI.motivation: AML and trade surveillance are largely manual and rule-based, with over 95% of alerts estimated to be false positives that burden human analysts. The authors seek to test whether quantum and hybrid classifiers can offer a viable alternative on a realistic detection task.
AI.method: Like-for-like benchmark of four quantum/hybrid models: (1) fidelity-based quantum k-NN with clustering-based routing; (2) QSVM on a one-body projected quantum kernel; (3) 20-qubit QNN with Pauli-ZZ feature map and RealAmplitudes ansatz; (4) HQNN where a small classical network generates all rotation angles of a 5-qubit circuit. Baselines: logistic regression, XGBoost, 1- and 3-hidden-layer NNs, classical k-NN. Shared stratified split of 1000 accounts (800/200, 20% suspicious) and two 20-feature representations (ANOVA, PCA); QKNN/QSVM tested under simulated noise and HQNN run on ibm_fez.
AI.result: Best overall is XGBoost on ANOVA features (suspicious-class F1 = 61.4%). HQNN is strongest quantum-hybrid (54.5–57.9% ideal simulator, 55.4–59.8% on ibm_fez), beating six of eight classical configurations; at 15% FPR, half its alerts are genuine. It outperforms QNN (42.0% F1) with under half the false alarms at similar recall and a quarter of the qubits. QKNN reaches 43.5% F1 (44.4% under noise) vs classical KNN 35.6%; QSVM maxes at 41%.
AI.conclusion: No quantum advantage is observed, but a five-qubit hybrid on current NISQ hardware already matches well-tuned classical models, with headroom via richer circuits and larger devices. The work contributes a rigorous like-for-like comparison on shared data, splits and features.

title: Control-Noise Trade-offs in Industrially Integrated ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ Spin-1/2 Qubits
comment: 28 pages, 4 main figures and 5 extended data figures
summary: Scaling silicon spin qubits to fault-tolerant processors requires semiconductor foundry integration, yet it remains unclear how industrial fabrication and dense device integration affect qubit control and noise. Here we study ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ electron spin-1/2 qubits fabricated using Intel's industry-compatible 300 mm process and incorporating micromagnets for electrically driven spin resonance, using a high-performance device fabricated in the RIKEN research cleanroom as a reference. Primitive $π/2$-gate fidelities reach the 99.99% level in the Intel devices, which also exhibit longer idle coherence, weaker low-frequency correlations and reduced qubit-to-qubit variability across several measured characteristics. In the present Intel devices, the micromagnets are integrated inline with the back-end-of-line (BEOL) contact routing, with their separation from the quantum well set through the vertical stack design. Relative to the reference, their larger separation contributes to weaker longitudinal and transverse magnetic-field gradients. The weaker longitudinal gradient suppresses the conversion of charge noise into qubit-frequency fluctuations, whereas the weaker transverse gradient reduces electrically driven spin-resonance efficiency and makes drive-dependent errors relevant at lower Rabi frequencies. Additional BEOL routing and metal levels required for two-dimensional arrays make such placement decisions increasingly consequential when scaling. These results establish an integration-level control-noise trade-off linking micromagnet placement within densely routed layouts to achievable gate performance, while very high-fidelity operation remains possible in industrially fabricated devices.

AI.tldr: Intel's 300 mm industry-fabricated 28Si/SiGe spin qubits reach 99.99% primitive π/2-gate fidelity and outperform a RIKEN reference device, but BEOL-integrated micromagnets positioned farther from the quantum well weaken field gradients, creating an integration-level control-noise trade-off.
AI.motivation: Scaling silicon spin qubits to fault-tolerant processors demands semiconductor foundry integration, but the impact of industrial fabrication and dense device integration on qubit control and noise is unclear.
AI.method: Studies 28Si/SiGe electron spin-1/2 qubits fabricated with Intel's industry-compatible 300 mm process, with micromagnets integrated inline in the BEOL contact routing and their quantum-well separation set by the vertical stack; compares against a high-performance reference device from the RIKEN research cleanroom.
AI.result: Intel devices achieve primitive π/2-gate fidelities at the 99.99% level, with longer idle coherence, weaker low-frequency correlations, and reduced qubit-to-qubit variability. Their larger micromagnet–quantum-well separation yields weaker longitudinal and transverse field gradients: the weaker longitudinal gradient suppresses charge-noise-to-qubit-frequency conversion, while the weaker transverse gradient reduces electrically driven spin-resonance efficiency, making drive-dependent errors relevant at lower Rabi frequencies.
AI.conclusion: Establishes an integration-level control-noise trade-off linking micromagnet placement within densely routed layouts to achievable gate performance, noting that additional BEOL routing and metal levels for 2D arrays make such placement decisions increasingly consequential, while very high-fidelity operation remains feasible in industrially fabricated devices.

title: Lifting the mixed to the pure: quantum phases of matter from canonical purification
summary: Pure-state quantum phases are defined through finite-depth local unitary connections. This concept of phases has recently been generalized to mixed states in terms of locally reversible channels. In this work, we establish a fundamental relation between mixed-state phases and pure-state phases. We show that a locally reversible channel between mixed states can be lifted to a local isometry between their canonical purifications; thus, if two mixed states are in the same phase, then their canonical purifications are in the same pure-state phase. Furthermore, an explicit construction of the lifting isometry is given by ``half'' of the Petz recovery map, suggesting that the Petz recovery map \emph{without rotation} is enough to connect mixed state phases. We illustrate our results with two examples: toric code under bit flip noise and Chern insulator under fermion number noise.

AI.tldr: Locally reversible channels connecting mixed states lift to local isometries between their canonical purifications, so equal mixed-state phase implies equal pure-state phase of purifications; the lifting isometry is half the Petz recovery map.
AI.motivation: Pure-state phases are defined via finite-depth local unitary connections, and this notion was recently extended to mixed states via locally reversible channels. The relationship between these two notions of phase—mixed-state phases and pure-state phases—was previously unclear; the paper aims to establish a fundamental link between them.
AI.method: Show that a locally reversible channel between two mixed states can be lifted to a local isometry between their canonical purifications, and construct this lifting isometry explicitly as "half" of the Petz recovery map, arguing that the Petz recovery map without rotation suffices to connect mixed-state phases. Illustrate with the toric code under bit-flip noise and the Chern insulator under fermion-number noise.
AI.result: If two mixed states are in the same mixed-state phase, their canonical purifications are in the same pure-state phase. An explicit lifting isometry is given by half the Petz recovery map, indicating the unrotated Petz recovery map is adequate for connecting mixed-state phases. The two examples (toric code with bit-flip noise, Chern insulator with fermion-number noise) illustrate the result.
AI.conclusion: Mixed-state phases are fundamentally tied to pure-state phases through canonical purifications: locally reversible channel connections lift to local isometry connections between purifications. This provides a purification-based bridge between the two phase classifications and identifies the Petz recovery map as the natural connecting object.

title: Locality, Probability and the Relevance of History
summary: Relativistic theory and experiments teach us that causal influences are constrained by the speed of light. Deterministic theories incorporate this lesson in $\textit{functional}$ terms: whether an event occurs or not is functionally determined by events that occur in its immediate causal past. In this paper we suggest a natural generalization of this constraint that applies to probabilistic theories: the $\textit{probability}$ that an event occurs is to be functionally determined by the $\textit{probability}$ of the event-occurrences in its immediate causal past. This constraint differs from Bell's criterion of local causality and turns out to imply it only under an additional assumption that requires history to be, in a sense, $\textit{ir}$relevant. Bell-inequality-violating quantum phenomena are thus arguably $\textit{not}$ in tension with relativity, locality, "statistical independence", nor with a supposed "realism". What they instead show is that history is, in a sense, $\textit{relevant}$.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that causal influences are constrained by the speed of light: whether an event occurs is functionally determined by immediate causal past events.
AI.motivation: Relativistic theory and experiments constrain causal influences by the speed of light.
AI.method: Generalizes the functional constraint to probabilistic theories: probability of an event is functionally determined by probabilities of immediate causal-past events; compares with Bell's local causality criterion.
AI.result: The new constraint differs from Bell's local causality and implies it only under an added assumption that history is irrelevant; Bell-violating phenomena are not in tension with relativity/locality/realism but show history is relevant.
AI.conclusion: Bell-inequality-violating quantum phenomena are arguably not in tension with relativity, locality, statistical independence, nor realism; what they show is that history is, in a sense, relevant.

title: GENIE: learned quantum circuits as embedding impurity solvers, and why compactness, not correlation strength, decides when they work
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures. Code: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23736693; data: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23737678
summary: Sample-based quantum diagonalization has been used as an impurity solver in density matrix embedding theory (DMET), but always with fixed-form circuits and without comparison to classical selection at the same subspace size. We introduce GENIE, a DMET impurity solver in which a generative transformer learns the sampling circuit, trained on the quantum-selected configuration interaction energy. On N2, hydrogen chains, water and a hydrogen ring, we compare GENIE at equal determinant budget with classical selected configuration interaction (CIPSI, ASCI, heat-bath CI) and with DMET combined with sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). GENIE selects: for N2 at 200 determinants it is within a factor of 1.7 of CIPSI and 25 to 1000 times more accurate than the determinants a fixed circuit actually samples, while standard SQD reaches good energies mainly by filling the subspace. GENIE does not beat the best classical selection, and its circuits require fault-tolerant hardware. Its failures are governed by the compactness of the wavefunction relative to the budget, not by correlation strength. A cheap estimate from coupled-cluster amplitudes predicts this compactness. A router built on it never recommended GENIE where it then failed, apart from seed-to-seed variance, and it transferred unchanged to a blind test on new systems. We also identify two benchmarking pitfalls that can create apparent quantum advantages of one to two orders of magnitude.

AI.tldr: GENIE is a generative-transformer-learned DMET impurity solver trained on quantum-selected CI energy; at equal determinant budgets it nears but does not beat the best classical selection (CIPSI/ASCI/heat-bath CI), and its failures are predictable from wavefunction compactness via coupled-cluster amplitudes.
AI.motivation: Sample-based quantum diagonalization has been used as a DMET impurity solver but only with fixed-form circuits and without comparison to classical selection at matched subspace size, leaving the practical value of learned quantum sampling unclear.
AI.method: Introduce GENIE, a DMET impurity solver where a generative transformer learns the sampling circuit, trained on the quantum-selected configuration interaction energy. Compare at equal determinant budget against classical selected CI (CIPSI, ASCI, heat-bath CI) and against DMET+SQD on N2, hydrogen chains, water and a hydrogen ring. A cheap compactness estimate from coupled-cluster amplitudes is used to build a router.
AI.result: On N2 at 200 determinants, GENIE is within a factor of 1.7 of CIPSI and 25–1000x more accurate than determinants sampled by a fixed circuit, while standard SQD reaches good energies mainly by filling the subspace. GENIE does not beat the best classical selection and requires fault-tolerant hardware. Failures are governed by wavefunction compactness relative to the budget, not correlation strength. The coupled-cluster-based router never recommended GENIE where it subsequently failed (apart from seed-to-seed variance) and transferred unchanged to a blind test on new systems. Two benchmarking pitfalls that can fabricate apparent quantum advantages of one to two orders of magnitude are identified.
AI.conclusion: Learned quantum sampling is competitive but not superior to classical selected CI at matched budget; its applicability is predictable from a cheap compactness diagnostic, and benchmark protocols must avoid pitfalls that inflate apparent quantum advantage.

title: No generalised contextuality from the vacuum
summary: We show that, under certain conditions, generalised contextuality, in the sense introduced by Spekkens, cannot be created from the vacuum of a quantum field. Initial noncontextual qudit states do not become contextual just by interacting with a quantum field. This is verified in two scenarios. First, in a perturbative approach where the time evolution operator is expanded in powers of the coupling constant. Second, in the limit of zero energy gap in the spectrum of the free detector Hamiltonian. Our results are at the opposite side of what has been recently obtained in the literature regarding the harvesting of Kochen-Specker contextuality. Our results demonstrate that the existing notions of contextuality can be independent of one another and that contextuality harvesting depends on which precise notion is used.

AI.tldr: Under certain conditions, generalized (Spekkens) contextuality cannot be created from the vacuum of a quantum field: initially noncontextual qudit states stay noncontextual after interacting with the field, unlike recent claims for Kochen-Specker contextuality harvesting.
AI.motivation: Recent literature reports harvesting of Kochen-Specker contextuality from the quantum vacuum; the authors test whether the same holds for the distinct notion of generalized (Spekkens) contextuality, probing how notion-dependent such harvesting phenomena are.
AI.method: Two scenarios are analyzed for a qudit detector interacting with a quantum field: (i) a perturbative treatment expanding the time-evolution operator in powers of the coupling constant, and (ii) the limit of vanishing energy gap in the free detector Hamiltonian spectrum.
AI.result: In both scenarios, initially noncontextual qudit states do not become generalized-contextual through interaction with the field, i.e., generalized contextuality cannot be created from the vacuum.
AI.conclusion: The findings contrast with recent Kochen-Specker contextuality harvesting results, showing that existing notions of contextuality can be independent of one another and that contextuality harvesting depends on which precise notion is employed.

title: Resource efficient Sample Based Quantum Simulation through Fragmentation and Virtual Partitioning of QPU
summary: Present-day sample-based quantum algorithms within quantum-centric supercomputing workflows require substantial classical post-processing, large circuit depths to produce chemically relevant samples, and long QPU times to execute the many circuits needed for molecules of chemically relevant size. We introduce FMO-QVM-HCI-HSQD, a resource-efficient sample-based framework that breaks a large problem into fragments, runs the fragments in parallel on virtual regions of the QPU, and reduces circuit depth through a half-qubit ansatz whose samples seed an HCI expansion. We demonstrate the algorithm on ibm_marrakesh and ibm_boston for the water trimer and the carmofur_Mpro complex with up to 52 qubits, benchmarking against FMO-CCSD(T), FMO-CASCI and FMO-HCI. For the water trimer (14 spin orbitals for monomers, 28 for dimers), our method reduces the two-qubit depth by 39% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD and the QPU time by 82% compared to sequential FMO-SQD, and accesses 3% of the determinant subspace versus 40% for FMO-SQD, while achieving more accurate energies. For the carmofur_Mpro complex (16 and 32 spin orbitals), it reduces the two-qubit depth by 47% and the QPU time by 20% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD, and accesses 0.007% of the determinant subspace versus 40%, while remaining within chemical accuracy. Extending the carmofur_Mpro active space in the 6-31G basis to 52 and 104 spin orbitals, sampled on 26 and 52 qubits, the total energy deviates from FMO-HCI by only 1.22 mHa. These results show that combining fragmentation, virtual QPU partitioning and half-qubit sampling makes sample-based quantum simulation of chemically relevant systems feasible on current hardware.

AI.tldr: FMO-QVM-HCI-HSQD: a fragment-based, resource-efficient sample-based quantum framework using half-qubit ansatz + HCI to enable chemically relevant quantum simulation on current hardware.
AI.motivation: Sample-based quantum algorithms in quantum-centric supercomputing need heavy classical post-processing, large circuit depths for chemically relevant samples, and long QPU times—making them impractical for chemically relevant molecular sizes.
AI.method: Combines fragment molecular orbital (FMO) fragmentation, parallel execution on virtual QPU regions, a half-qubit ansatz that halves circuit depth, and half-qubit-seeded HCI expansion to reduce determinant-subspace sampling. Tested on ibm_marrakesh and ibm_boston for water trimer and carmofur_Mpro (up to 52 qubits), benchmarked against FMO-CCSD(T), FMO-CASCI, and FMO-HCI.
AI.result: Water trimer (14/28 spin orbitals): 39% lower two-qubit depth vs FMO-QVM-SQD, 82% less QPU time vs sequential FMO-SQD, 3% vs 40% determinant subspace, with higher accuracy. Carmofur_Mpro (16/32 spin orbitals): 47% lower two-qubit depth, 20% less QPU time, 0.007% vs 40% subspace, within chemical accuracy. Extended to 52/104 spin orbitals (26/52 qubits): 1.22 mHa deviation from FMO-HCI.
AI.conclusion: Combining fragmentation, virtual QPU partitioning, and half-qubit sampling makes sample-based quantum simulation of chemically relevant systems feasible on current hardware.

title: Logical Bell Inequalities for Marginal Wigner Negativity
summary: We construct logical Bell inequalities whose violations are determined by the Wigner function of a reduced quantum state. For odd-prime qudits, each phase-space point of any nonempty proper subsystem defines an inequality, violated precisely when the corresponding Gross Wigner value is negative. This correspondence allows us to quantify the contextuality that a reduced state guarantees for the composite system. The normalized violation gives a lower bound on the contextual fraction in the complete Weyl measurement scenario, valid for every joint state with that marginal, irrespective of its correlations. We identify a family of product states that saturates this bound. For these states, one marginal Wigner value fixes the contextual fraction of the entire system.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs logical Bell inequalities whose violations for odd-prime qudits are governed by the Gross Wigner function of a reduced state, yielding a lower bound on the contextual fraction of any joint state with that marginal, and identifies product states saturating this bound.
AI.motivation: Negativity of the Wigner function signals nonclassicality, and contextuality is a resource that a subsystem can guarantee for a composite system. The authors seek a direct, quantitative link between the phase-space (Wigner) description of a reduced state and the contextuality that marginal enforces on the whole system.
AI.method: For odd-prime qudits, logical Bell inequalities are associated with each phase-space point of any nonempty proper subsystem. These inequalities are violated exactly when the corresponding Gross Wigner value is negative. The normalized violation is then used to bound the contextual fraction in the complete Weyl measurement scenario, valid for all joint states sharing the given marginal.
AI.result: Each phase-space point of any nonempty proper subsystem yields an inequality violated precisely at negativity of the corresponding Gross Wigner value. The normalized violation gives a lower bound on the contextual fraction valid for every joint state with that marginal, and a family of product states saturating the bound is identified, for which a single marginal Wigner value fixes the contextual fraction of the whole system.
AI.conclusion: Gross Wigner negativity of a reduced state maps one-to-one onto violation of logical Bell inequalities, providing a marginal-based lower bound on contextuality of composite systems, tight for a family of product states where the marginal Wigner value fully determines the contextual fraction.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Classification: A Comparative Study with Classical Kernels
summary: Quantum kernel methods are the most concrete near-term proposal for quantum machine learning on classical data, yet published benchmarks disagree on whether they outperform tuned classical kernels, and the disagreement cannot be resolved from the literature because the comparisons are not protocol-controlled. We argue that the obstacle is one of measurement, not theory: the usual setup fixes the quantum feature map's data scaling while grid-searching the classical kernel's hyperparameters, recomputes nothing per fold, and reports cost in simulator time. We therefore treat the comparison itself as the object of study and impose three controls. The bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical $γ$, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations. On top of these we run a factorial design of 324 cells in which dimensionality, training size, class separability and data structure are explicit covariates, together with four standard datasets, a shots-versus-gate-noise ablation, and a cost sweep. The dominant effect we measure is not quantum: tuning the feature map's bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data, exceeding every quantum-classical difference we observe. Tuned quantum kernels are then statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on all four real datasets. The advantage on synthetic data is confined almost entirely to data generated by the feature map itself, and it shrinks with dimensionality (-0.0045 per qubit) while growing with sample size. Finite sampling costs an order of magnitude more accuracy than gate and readout noise, and a fidelity kernel needs $5\times10^{7}$ circuits at n = 10,000. Protocol variance is thus sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions.

AI.tldr: Published quantum-kernel benchmarks conflict because their comparisons are not protocol-controlled. Re-running the comparison with bandwidth tuning, per-fold recomputation, and hardware-cost accounting shows the dominant effect is bandwidth tuning, not quantum advantage; tuned quantum kernels are statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on four real datasets.
AI.motivation: Quantum kernel methods are the most concrete near-term proposal for quantum machine learning on classical data, yet published benchmarks disagree on whether they beat tuned classical kernels. Because comparisons in the literature are not protocol-controlled, the disagreement cannot be resolved from prior work. The authors argue the obstacle is measurement rather than theory, and make the comparison itself the object of study.
AI.method: Three protocol controls are imposed: (1) the quantum feature map's bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical RBF's gamma; (2) the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing; (3) cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations rather than simulator time. On top of these, a factorial design of 324 cells treats dimensionality, training size, class separability, and data structure as explicit covariates, supplemented by four standard datasets, a shots-versus-gate-noise ablation, and a cost sweep.
AI.result: The dominant measured effect is not quantum: tuning the feature-map bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data, exceeding every quantum-classical difference observed. Tuned quantum kernels are statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on all four real datasets. The synthetic advantage is confined almost entirely to data generated by the feature map itself, shrinks with dimensionality (-0.0045 per qubit), and grows with sample size. Finite sampling costs an order of magnitude more accuracy than gate and readout noise, and a fidelity kernel requires 5e7 circuits at n = 10,000.
AI.conclusion: Protocol variance is sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions. Apparent quantum advantages reported in prior work are attributable to uncontrolled protocol differences rather than genuine performance gains, so future benchmarks must control bandwidth tuning, per-fold recomputation, and hardware-level cost accounting.

title: Benchmarking Single-Photon Sources for Measurement-Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution
summary: Measurement-Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (MDI-QKD) enables secure communication without trusting the measurement devices, but its performance critically depends on the quality of the employed photon sources. We compare MDI-QKD implementations based on Weak Coherent Pulses (WCPs) with those employing Quantum Dot (QD) single-photon sources. WCP-based schemes are fundamentally limited by Poissonian photon-number statistics, imposing a trade-off between single- and multi-photon emissions, whereas QD sources exhibit sub-Poissonian statistics with low antibunching parameter $g^{(2)}(0)$. Using a decoy-state analysis for both source types, we find that even at moderate mean photon numbers, QD-based implementations outperform the best-case WCP configuration - where the mean photon number is optimised at each transmission distance - across the full range of transmission distances. We further incorporate the effect of imperfect photon indistinguishability via Hong-Ou-Mandel interference visibilities into the security framework and demonstrate that both source types are highly sensitive to even small deviations from ideal indistinguishability, significantly affecting achievable key rates and maximum transmission distance.

AI.tldr: Quantum dot single-photon sources outperform optimized weak coherent pulses in MDI-QKD across all transmission distances, and both source types are highly sensitive to imperfect photon indistinguishability.
AI.motivation: MDI-QKD removes the need to trust measurement devices, but its performance is limited by photon source quality; the authors aim to quantify how source photon-number statistics and indistinguishability degrade key rates and range.
AI.method: Comparison of MDI-QKD with weak coherent pulses (Poissonian statistics, decoy-state analysis) versus quantum dot single-photon sources (sub-Poissonian, low antibunching g^(2)(0)); WCP mean photon number optimized per distance; imperfect indistinguishability incorporated via Hong-Ou-Mandel interference visibilities in the security analysis.
AI.result: QD-based MDI-QKD outperforms the best-case optimized WCP configuration across the full range of transmission distances, even at moderate mean photon numbers; both source types are highly sensitive to small deviations from ideal indistinguishability, significantly reducing achievable key rates and maximum transmission distance.
AI.conclusion: Quantum dot single-photon sources are a superior choice for MDI-QKD, but realizing this advantage requires near-ideal photon indistinguishability, making HOM visibility a critical design parameter for practical implementations.

title: The Quartic Gap Between Quantum and Dequantized Algorithms for Linear Algebra Is Tight
summary: Quantum algorithms for linear algebra that access a matrix $A$ through quantum random access memory (QRAM) prepare quantum states proportional to the solutions of linear systems and related problems. Dequantized classical algorithms, when given sampling and query access to $A$, return sampling and query access to an approximate solution. Both kinds of algorithms use a number of queries that is polynomial in the normalized Frobenius norm $ρ=\|A\|_F/\|A\|$ and does not directly depend on the dimension. For linear systems at fixed condition number and accuracy, quantum algorithms use $\widetilde O(ρ)$ queries, whereas the best dequantized algorithms use $\widetilde O(ρ^4)$. We prove that this quartic gap is tight in the worst case, up to a logarithmic factor. For every constant $κ_0>1$, we construct dense linear systems with condition number at most $κ_0$ for which sampling from the solution within a sufficiently small constant total variation distance requires $Ω(ρ^4/\logρ)$ classical queries but only $Θ(ρ)$ quantum queries. The same separation holds, for errors below smaller thresholds, for positive-definite systems, least squares, ridge regression, matrix powers and square roots, imaginary-time and real-time Hamiltonian evolution, and sampling from the top principal component. Our results therefore show that many quantum algorithms for linear algebra, achieve a near-quartic speedup in the worst case, over classical algorithms with sampling and query access. All of these classical lower bounds follow from the same framework, which is based on a lower bound for sampling from distributions that depend on a fixed set of Fourier coefficients of an unknown Boolean function.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the quartic query-complexity gap between quantum linear-algebra algorithms (Û(ρ) queries) and dequantized classical algorithms (Û(ρ⁴)) with sampling and query access is worst-case tight, up to logarithmic factors, and extends this separation to many related linear-algebra tasks.
AI.motivation: Quantum linear-algebra algorithms using QRAM achieve Û(ρ) queries where ρ is the normalized Frobenius norm, while dequantized classical algorithms with sample/query access require Û(ρ⁴). The community lacked a proof that this quartic gap is necessary—i.e., that no better dequantized algorithm exists—so the tightness of the separation was an open question.
AI.method: The authors construct, for every constant κ₀>1, dense linear systems with condition number at most κ₀, and derive classical lower bounds via a unified framework based on a lower bound for sampling from distributions that depend on a fixed set of Fourier coefficients of an unknown Boolean function. Quantum upper bounds (Θ(ρ)) are matched against these classical lower bounds (Ω(ρ⁴/log ρ)).
AI.result: For these constructed dense systems, sampling from the solution within a sufficiently small constant total variation distance requires Ω(ρ⁴/log ρ) classical queries but only Θ(ρ) quantum queries, establishing the quartic gap is tight up to a logarithmic factor. The same separation holds for positive-definite systems, least squares, ridge regression, matrix powers and square roots, imaginary-time and real-time Hamiltonian evolution, and sampling from the top principal component.
AI.conclusion: Many quantum linear-algebra algorithms achieve a near-quartic worst-case speedup over classical algorithms with sampling and query access, and all the classical lower bounds derive from a single Fourier-coefficient-based sampling framework.

title: Topologically Protected Edge States in a Single Flux Qubit
summary: We show that topological edge states can be realized in a simple superconducting circuit composed of an inductively shunted flux qubit. The Josephson potential of that qubit forms a honeycomb lattice similar to the case of graphene. The additional shunting element produces a quartic potential along one flux direction, which effectively creates a boundary in flux space. We map analytically the low-energy dynamics of the circuit to an extended Su--Schrieffer--Heeger (SSH) chain, in which a quartic potential is added to the usual SSH Hamiltonian. This mapping is confirmed by numerical simulations of the full superconducting circuit. We argue that chiral symmetry still holds for the edge states of the extended model around a chiral point in parameter space. Close to this point, we numerically find that edge states in our superconducting circuit are topologically protected against perturbations that obey chiral symmetry, as is the case for charge noise. Our results show that topological effects previously thought to occur in multi-qubit systems, such as protection against decoherence, can also be found in much simpler single superconducting qubits.

AI.tldr: Topological edge states are shown to emerge in a single inductively shunted flux qubit, whose Josephson potential forms a graphene-like honeycomb lattice with a quartic boundary in flux space; the circuit maps to an extended SSH chain exhibiting chirally protected edge states.
AI.motivation: Topological protection against decoherence is conventionally associated with multi-qubit systems, which are complex to build. The authors aim to show that comparable topological effects can arise in a much simpler single superconducting qubit, motivating the search for topological edge states within one circuit.
AI.method: The system is an inductively shunted flux qubit. Its Josephson potential yields a honeycomb lattice analogous to graphene, while the shunt produces a quartic potential along one flux direction that acts as an effective boundary in flux space. The low-energy dynamics are analytically mapped onto an extended SSH chain (SSH Hamiltonian plus quartic term), and the mapping is validated by numerical simulation of the full circuit. Chiral symmetry of the edge states is analyzed around a chiral point in parameter space, and protection against symmetry-preserving perturbations such as charge noise is tested numerically.
AI.result: The analytical mapping to the extended SSH chain is confirmed by full-circuit simulations. Chiral symmetry is argued to persist for edge states near a chiral point, and numerical results show the edge states are topologically protected against perturbations obeying chiral symmetry, including charge noise.
AI.conclusion: Topological effects previously thought to require multi-qubit architectures, notably protection against decoherence, can be realized in a simple single superconducting qubit, opening a route to compact topologically protected quantum hardware.

title: Weighted hypergraph states as a resource for quantum metrology
summary: Quantum correlations can be used to improve sensing precision beyond classical limits, yet the correlated resource states needed can be challenging to prepare and preserve. Here, we study the family of weighted hypergraph states and identify subclasses characterized by their underlying graph topology that exhibit enhanced metrological performance. Using the quantum Fisher information and a novel Dicke state basis representation, we show that these subclasses outperform both separable and standard weighted graph state benchmarks over broad ranges of edge weights corresponding to weak controlled operations between qubits representing the vertices of the graph. We provide analytical formulas for an arbitrary number $N$ of qubits, supplemented by a general study, while focusing a detailed analysis on the example case of $N=4$. By identifying the critical probabilities for local dephasing, we show that adding higher-order weighted hyperedges for $N$ qubits can enhance metrological robustness, allowing the resulting states to retain a quantum advantage at higher noise levels. These probe states exhibit favorable scaling, enhanced precision, and noise tolerance. Our findings establish weighted hypergraph states as viable, structurally tunable and robust resources for quantum-enhanced metrology.

AI.tldr: Weighted hypergraph states in specific graph-topology subclasses outperform separable and standard weighted graph states as metrological probes over broad weak-edge-weight regimes, and higher-order hyperedges improve robustness against local dephasing.
AI.motivation: Quantum correlations can surpass classical sensing limits, but the required correlated resource states are hard to prepare and preserve. The authors seek structurally tunable, robust resource states for quantum-enhanced metrology.
AI.method: The study analyzes the family of weighted hypergraph states and identifies subclasses by underlying graph topology. It uses the quantum Fisher information plus a novel Dicke-state basis representation, derives analytical formulas for arbitrary qubit number N (with detailed N=4 analysis), and computes critical probabilities for local dephasing to assess noise robustness.
AI.result: The identified topological subclasses outperform separable states and standard weighted graph state benchmarks across broad ranges of edge weights corresponding to weak controlled operations. Analytical formulas hold for arbitrary N. Adding higher-order weighted hyperedges raises the critical dephasing probability, so states retain quantum advantage at higher noise levels, with favorable scaling, enhanced precision, and noise tolerance.
AI.conclusion: Weighted hypergraph states are viable, structurally tunable, and robust resources for quantum-enhanced metrology.

title: Time-optimal quantum dynamics under fixed-norm generators
summary: We investigate the dynamics of quantum systems whose evolution is governed by linear generators of fixed unitarily invariant norm. For this broad class of evolutions, we derive a universal time-optimal generator of the dynamics converting one given state into another. It provides a time-optimal non-Hermitian Hamiltonian for pure state conversion. We then use this general result to derive quantum speed limits for mixed-state evolutions governed by Lindbladians and non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. Our findings follow from the geometric properties of the group $GL(n,\mathbb{C})$, in particular the geodesic distance. The derived bounds hold for an arbitrary system size $n$, depend only on the norms of the evolution generator and the initial and final states, and do not require performing any time-averaging.

AI.tldr: The authors derive a universal time-optimal generator (of fixed unitarily invariant norm) for converting one quantum state into another, yielding a time-optimal non-Hermitian Hamiltonian for pure-state conversion, and use it to obtain quantum speed limits for mixed-state evolutions governed by Lindbladians and non-Hermitian Hamiltonians via the geodesic geometry of GL(n,C).
AI.motivation: Existing quantum speed limits often depend on system size, require time-averaging, or are tailored to specific evolution types. The authors seek universal, size-independent bounds that depend only on the norm of the evolution generator and the initial/final states, applicable to a broad class of evolutions governed by linear generators of fixed unitarily invariant norm.
AI.method: They exploit the geometric properties of the group GL(n,C), in particular its geodesic distance, to construct a universal time-optimal generator of the dynamics. This general result is then applied to derive quantum speed limits for mixed-state evolutions under Lindbladians and non-Hermitian Hamiltonians.

title: Secret-shared teleportation of a two-qudit gate with a deferred recipient
summary: An unknown quantum operation, like an unknown quantum state, cannot be perfectly copied or stored for later use. A specific gate can be embedded in an entangled resource and teleported, but its destination is fixed when the resource is created. Here we show that the capability to apply a two-qudit entangling gate can instead be secret-shared among many parties: the shares are distributed in advance, and a later key release lets exactly one of them, chosen after distribution, exercise it. A provider encrypts half of a Bell pair held with a user into $n$ shares, one per candidate node. The selected node, given the key qudits, completes an exact non-local $\mathtt{CSUM}^{k}$ gate with the user's data, in every measurement branch and for any qudit dimension, with the power $k$ chosen by the user alone. Any coalition of fewer than $n$ candidate nodes, or the key register alone, holds no information, unselected nodes cannot tell whether a selection occurred, and the key cannot decrypt twice. For two candidates the registers form a $((3,5))$ threshold scheme. Encoder and decoder are explicit $O(n)$ circuits. The construction supports jointly authorized and anonymous gate application, advancing distributed quantum computing and quantum network capabilities.
